CITY OF INGLEWOOD
  DEVELOPMENT SERVICES DEPARTMENT
  PLANNING DIVISION
  PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING AGENDA
February 5, 2025, 7:00 P.M.
City Council Chambers – Ninth Floor
1 West Manchester Boulevard

1.  Pledge of Allegiance.

2.  Roll Call.

3.  Communications from staff.

4.  Public Comments Regarding Agenda Items. Persons wishing to address
  the Planning Commission on any item on the agenda other than a
  public hearing may do so at this time.

5.  Minute(s) approval for December 4, 2024, and January 14, 2025,
  Planning Commission meeting(s).

6.  PUBLIC HEARINGS:
  a. A public hearing to consider an application by Gary Le for
  Special Use Permit No. 24-00026 (SUP24-00026) to allow the
  expansion of a drive-thru and construct a 30 square-foot
  addition to an existing 3,615 square-foot free-standing fast-
  food restaurant that is part of a shopping center on an
  approximately 58,797 square-foot H-C (Historic Core) property
  at 401 East Manchester Boulevard.
  The applicant has requested that this item be continued to the
  March 5, 2025 Planning Commission meeting.

  b. A public hearing to consider an application Chima Chibueze
  representing the Tribe for a Special Use Permit No. 24-00027
  (SUP24-00027) to to allow hookah tobacco use for an existing
  bar/nightclub on an approximately 34,600 square-foot, MU-1 (TOD
  Mixed Use-1) zoned property at 446 South Market Street.

  Preliminary Recommendations:
  A. If the Planning Commission determines to APPROVE the
  request, it is recommended to:
  1) Affirm the categorical exemption EA-CE-2025-001;
  2) Adopt the resolution approving SUP24-00027.
  B. If the Planning Commission determines to ADD CONDITIONS,
  it is recommended to:
  1) Take the above actions but modify the number of
  conditions as appropriate.
  C. If the Planning Commission determines to DENY the request
  or any part thereof, it is recommended to:
  1) Take the appropriate actions and make the findings.

7.  NON-PUBLIC HEARING:
  a. A non-public hearing to consider an application by Real Estate
  Development Services Group for Final Tract Map No. 84423 (FTM-
  84423) to allow the subdivision of air rights for the development
  of  five  units,  two-and-one-half-story,  townhome-style
  condominiums on an approximately 8,006 square-foot R-3
  (Multiple-family Residential) zoned property at 419 South
  Eucalyptus Avenue.

  Planning Commission Actions:
  A. If the Planning Commission determines to APPROVE the
  request, it is recommended to:
  1) Adopt the resolution recommending approval of FTM-84423
  by the Mayor and City Council; and
   B. If the Planning Commission determines to DENY the request
  or any part thereof, it is recommended to:
  1) Take the above actions and make the findings.

8.  Planning Commission Report- General Plan Existing Conditions
  Report, Community Profile, and Vision Statement and Guiding
  Principles.

  Planning Commission Action:
  A. Receive and File
  Item 8 Documents

9.  Public Comments. Anyone wishing to address the Planning Commission
  on any matter within their jurisdiction and not elsewhere
  considered on the agenda may do so at this time.

10.  Commission Initiatives.

11.  Adjournment.

If you require special accommodations due to a disability, please contact
the Planning Division at (310) 412-5230, One Manchester Boulevard, Fourth
Floor, Inglewood City Hall, Inglewood, CA 90301. All requests for special
accommodations must be received 48 hours prior to the day of the
hearing(s).

"Si no entiende esta noticia o si necesita más información, favor de
llamar a este número (310) 412-5230."

is not held or is concluded prior to a public hearing or other agenda
item being considered, the public hearing or non-public hearing agenda
item will automatically be continued to the next regular Planning
Commission meeting.

REQUEST
The applicant, Real Estate Development Services Group, is requesting approval of Final
Tract Map No. 84423 (FTM-84423) to allow the subdivision of air rights for the
development of five-units, two-and-one-half-story, townhome-style condominiums at 419
South Eucalyptus Avenue.

BACKGROUND
In accordance with the California State Subdivision Map Act and provisions of the
Inglewood Municipal Code (IMC), the Planning Commission must review all subdivision
applications and act upon tentative and final tract maps. A tract map is required for the
subdivision of a property into more than five lots or the creation of condominium units.
Since condominium units constitute a subdivision, in that air rights of the property are
subdivided and sold separately, the Commission must act on this subdivision map. If the
Planning Commission recommends the map for approval, it will go to the City Council for
review and final approval.

On May 6, 2022, Site Plan Review No. 2021-062 (PR-2021-062) was approved for the
request for a new five-unit, two-and-one-half-story residential apartment building.

On April 5, 2024, a Vesting Tentative Tract Map application for a townhome-style
condominium was filed.

On June 6, 2024, Public Works and the Subdivision Committee approved Vesting
Tentative Tract Map No. 84423 (VTTM-84423).

On August 7, 2024, the Planning Commission approved Vesting Tentative Tract Map No.
84423 (VTTM-84423) and was recommended to the City Council.

On August 27, 2024, a Certificate of Occupancy was issued for the five-unit building.

On September 17, 2024, the City Council approved Vesting Tentative Tract Map No.
84423 (VTTM-84423) subject to 9 conditions to allow for the creation of the five (5)
townhome-style condominiums.

DISCUSSION
Final Tract Map No. 84423 (FTM-84423) is a residential subdivision that will provide one
lot with five condominiums. The units will range in size from 1,244 to 1,432 square feet.
Each unit will provide the Code-required fully enclosed two-car garage. The table below
gives a breakdown of the square footage of each unit, the number of bedrooms, the
number of bathrooms, and private open space.

The Tract Map will subdivide the property into condominiums; each unit will be sold
separately, with the purchaser owning the unit outright and sharing common areas
(driveways, yards, etc.). Each owner will be a member of a Homeowners Association
that is responsible for the maintenance of the common areas through access easements
prescribed in the Final Tract Map. As required by the IMC subdivision regulations, a Final
Tract Map No. 84423 (VTTM-84423) was filed.

The applicant must adhere to all applicable local, state, and county regulations including
those of the State Department of Real Estate, California Energy Commission, the current
edition of the Uniform Building Code, and the Inglewood Municipal Code. In addition, the
applicant must record the Final Tract Map with the Los Angeles County Recorder’s office
prior to obtaining a Certificate of Occupancy from the City of Inglewood and prior to the
sale of the units.

Covenants, Conditions, and Restrictions (CC&Rs)
The applicant submitted a copy of the CC&Rs for the proposed condominium project for
the City’s review and approval. The CC&Rs contain rules and regulations that stipulate
the responsibilities of the homeowners association relative to the maintenance of the
common areas (landscaping, driveways, etc.) and improvements to the property.

General Plan Consistency
The proposed residential condominium project is consistent with the “Medium Density
Residential” designation of the Land Use Element of the Inglewood General Plan by
providing a variety of housing types and ownership opportunities.

The proposed project supports the following IMC goals:

Housing Element
   Stable and safe neighborhoods where housing is protected, rehabilitated, and
  modernized.
  o The condominiums are being constructed in a modern architectural style,
  which will help to modernize the neighborhood and provide more diversity
  in the city’s housing stock.
   A path to homeownership for local renters that strengthens the City’s
  neighborhoods and provides long-term stability to its population.

Vision and Guiding Principles – Jan 2025

VISION STATEMENT
The City of Inglewood, with our rich history and diverse culture, owes our return to success to our
residents, small businesses and economic partners. Community pride in the city's resurgent
national brand as a premier place to live, work, prosper and play is tangible and visible.
Inglewood’s vibrant residential neighborhoods and our diverse range of local services; accented
by our state of the art sports and entertainment venues; attract regional and international visitors
throughout the year. Inglewood is an inclusive community, where people walk, run, recreate and
actively participate in community events, both large and small. Inglewood is a city that cherishes
the concept of being good neighbors.

Inglewood’s Next Level will be defined by our ability to provide residents and visitors with a variety
of housing choices (both market rate and affordable), alongside desirable local shopping and
services. The Inglewood resurrection will continue to manifest itself in the abundant generation
of well-paying jobs for residents and surrounding cities and improved access to health care. The
Next Level will include quality schools, a continued emphasis on high quality recreation and
developmental services, well-maintained parks, and a safe, efficient transportation system to serve
a community that will accommodate 4.5 to 5 million visitors annually. The Next Level of Inglewood
is not just a vision; it is the continued manifestation resulting from the combination of intricate
strategy, planning and implementation processes (both broad and intricate) that have resulted in
the current Inglewood reality. That reality has birthed a thriving local economy where big and
small businesses for the most part blend seamlessly to serve both local residents and visitors from
all over the globe.

Inglewood's Next Level will be defined by our commitment to development practices grounded
in environmental sustainability, small business economic incubation and the promotion of high
levels of public safety; with a continued recognition of the need to promote social equity.

We will leave no residents behind as we embrace our self-imposed mandate of social and
economic self-determination. The City of Inglewood will continue to be a municipal leader, setting
the example for other cities to follow.

Vision and Guiding Principles – Jan 2025

GUIDING PRINCIPLES
Community Character
  • Accommodate uses, design development, and conduct events that celebrate, protect and
  build upon Inglewood’s history and embrace of art, education, diversity and cultures.
  • Seamlessly integrate and transition new buildings and development to reflect and
  maintain the scale and character of existing uses.
  • Develop attractive public streetscapes and plazas to entice high levels of pedestrian use
  and socialization.
  • Continue to emphasize public safety as a necessary quality of life component reflected in
  our development standards and other City programming.
  • Incrementally reduce visual blight and routinely maintain attractive public spaces and
  environments.

Growth and Development
  • Focus growth and development within existing centers and as infill and revitalization of
  commercial corridors.
  • Re-establish historic downtown Inglewood as the center of community identity and
  activity.
  • Support the development of uses that complement and provide synergy to maintain the
  vitality of economically active areas of the City.
  • Intensify and diversify development adjoining transit modes.
  • Enhance and improve existing commercial centers to develop amenities desired by
  residents.
  • Promote the re-use of economically obsolete and underutilized properties along
  commercial corridors.
  • Protect and expand housing opportunities for all ages, household types and income
  levels.

Community Facilities and Services
  • Maintain comprehensive education, social, health, and recreation services and programs
  to provide for the needs of residents of all ages and abilities.
  • Improve access to and distribution of parks and recreational amenities and support
  community arts, culture and events.

  1 INTRODUCTION
1.1 Content and Organization of the Existing
  Conditions Report
This document consists of nine chapters, as described below.

•  Chapter 1 Introduction. This chapter presents the legislative requirements for the General
  Plan, describes the city’s planning area, and outlines the contents of this document.

•  Chapter 2 Historic Resources. This chapter describes the historical development of
  Inglewood, including its early settlers, incorporation, land area and population growth, and
  key places and landmarks.

•  Chapter 3 Demographic and Economic Profile. This chapter provides information on the
  City’s demographic characteristics, economic conditions, tax revenues, and visitation trends.

•  Chapter 4 Market Analysis. This chapter presents an overview of broader market trends
  followed by the City's notable growth and development over the past five years and a detailed
  examination of the retail, office, industrial, multifamily, and hospitality sectors.

•  Chapter 5 Built Environment. This chapter contains an analysis of existing and planned land
  uses in the community, including an assessment of land use, community places, and urban
  form.

•  Chapter 6 Circulation. This chapter describes the City’s circulation systems, including its
  networks of roadways, transit services, pedestrian and bicycle infrastructure, and goods
  movement.

•  Chapter 7 Infrastructure. This chapter provides information regarding existing infrastructure,
  including water, sewer, storm drainage systems, and water quality programs.

•  Chapter 8 Public Services and Facilities. This chapter includes information on public services
  and facilities such as public parks and recreation programs, libraries, public schools, and police
  and fire services.

•  Chapter 9 The Natural Environment. This chapter describes the city’s biological resources,
  climate change impacts, air quality, geology and soils, hazards and hazardous materials,
  hydrology, and noise.

1.2 Overview
In late 2023, the City of Inglewood initiated the update of its General Plan, the first comprehensive

January 2025 | CITY OF INGLEWOOD | EXISTING CONDITIONS REPORT  Page 1-1
 Chapter 1 Introduction

update in several decades. The General Plan is organized into chapters, known as “elements.” This
update will include all elements required by State legislation that have not been updated recently
as well as optional elements to address specific priorities identified by the community, which
include Economic Development. The content of each of the mandated elements is prescribed by
California Government Code Section 65300 et seq., supplemented by guidelines published by the
Governor’s Office of Planning and Research.

The process of updating Inglewood’s General Plan is anticipated to involve seven principal stages:
1) documentation and analysis of existing conditions; 2) establishment of a community Vision
Statement that will guide the plan’s development; 3) preparation of the diagram depicting the
distribution of land uses to be permitted and standards for their intensity/density; 3) drafting of
goals, policies, and implementation programs for each plan element; 4) evaluation of the
environmental impacts of the updated plan as required by the California Environmental Quality
Act (CEQA); 5) publication of the updated General Plan and environmental document for public
review and comment; and 6) public hearings and adoption.

1.3 Purposes of the Existing Conditions Report
This document, the Existing Conditions Report, serves three important purposes for the General
Plan update process. First, it describes existing characteristics, needs, constraints, opportunities,
and future trends that serve as the foundation for developing the land use plan and goals, policies,
and implementation programs for each element. Each topic addressed in this report relates to
one or more of the required and optional plan elements. More than descriptions of the conditions
and trends for each topic, each section concludes with a discussion of the implications for
updating the plan. Second, many of these analyses provide benchmarks and metrics for testing
alternatives developed in the planning process as well as monitoring changes and the
effectiveness of updated policies post-adoption. Finally, information in this report provides the
substantive foundation for the “Existing Setting” section of the General Plan Environmental Impact
Report (EIR).

It is important to note that descriptions and analyses in this report are valid as of the date of its
publication in 2024. Some information is stable and will remain valid over an extended time, such
as seismic hazards and biological resources. Others will change, and may change frequently, such
as existing land use development and economic conditions. Consequently, it is important that the
database that contains this information be maintained, reviewed, and updated on a regular basis.
Text, graphics, and maps are documented as digital files to facilitate revisions as new information
is compiled. Because the database technically serves as an appendix to the General Plan, a CEQA-
based environmental review of its update is not required.

1.4 Background: Purposes/Legislative Requirements
  for the General Plan
The California Government Code (§ 65300) requires each city and county government to adopt a
comprehensive, long-term general plan. A general plan is a long-range policy document that sets

Page 1-2  CITY OF INGLEWOOD | EXISTING CONDITIONS REPORT | January 2025
   Chapter 1 Introduction

forth broad goals and objectives for the growth and development of a county or city. The general
plan must cover the land within the boundaries of the adopting city or county as well as “any land
outside its boundaries which in the planning agency’s judgment bears relation to its planning.”
Under State law, each general plan must contain eight elements—land use, circulation, housing,
conservation, open space, noise, safety, and environmental justice. There is no mandatory
structure or maximum number of elements, but all elements in a plan must be internally consistent
with one another. The general plan addresses a broad range of issues, and each element must set
objectives, principles, standards, and plan proposals for the long-term development of a county
or city.

1.5 Location and Planning Area
The city of Inglewood is in southwestern Los Angeles County, as shown on Figure 1-1. As shown
on Figure 1-2, it is generally bounded by the city of Los Angeles and the unincorporated Los
Angeles County communities of View Park-Windsor Hills and Ladera Heights to the north, the city
of Hawthorne and the unincorporated Los Angeles County community of Lennox to the south,
the city of Los Angeles to the west, and the unincorporated Los Angeles County community of
Westmont and the city of Los Angeles to the east. A small island of incorporated land is entirely
surrounded by the unincorporated community of Ladera Heights and city of Los Angeles in
proximity to the city’s northwest boundary. Inglewood’s sphere of influence, as determined by the
Los Angeles Local Agency Formation Commission, is generally coterminous with its jurisdictional
boundaries. However, the sphere of influence extends beyond the southern boundary of the city
to Lennox Boulevard. Access to Inglewood from the surrounding region and further afield is
provided by Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and Hawthorne Municipal Airport (HHR),
Interstates 405 and 105, the LA Metro K and C rail lines and several bus lines.

 Chapter 1 Introduction

1.6 Community Engagement
From June through October 2024, a robust program of community engagement was undertaken
by the General Plan update project team to inform community members about the update
process, solicit ideas for a long-term vision for the city, and supplement the technical analysis
conducted for the Existing Conditions Report with stakeholder observations of challenges and
opportunities present in the city today.

The program of public outreach encompassed a diversity of platforms and techniques. The project
team provided project information and solicited comments at multiple city events, including the
Juneteenth Celebration (6/16), Inglewood Music Festival (6/29), National Night Out (8/6), District
2 Chili Cook Off (8/17), District 1 Family Unity Day (8/24) and Hispanic Heritage Festival (9/21).
Citywide Open Houses were hosted in English and Spanish on September 14. Interviews were
conducted with stakeholder groups, including residents of each council district, business leaders,
non-profit and service providers, and members of the Planning Commission. A visioning survey in
English and Spanish was distributed by hand and made available online beginning June 12. The
City established a dedicated project web page where it published project information, solicited
sign-ups for a project notification list, and posted an informational video produced by City staff.
The project was also advertised on the City’s social media platforms and digital billboards citywide.
In addition, City staff provided regular updates to the Planning Commission and City Council.

More than 1,100 individual comments were collected via those various platforms. Each section of
the Existing Conditions Report, aside from Historic Resources, contains an overview of the key
themes raised in these comments as they relate to each of the topic areas.

  2 HISTORIC RESOURCES
Human occupation and settlement in Inglewood encompasses diverse and wide-ranging historic
narratives from precolonial times to the present day. The existing built environment includes
properties dating from the 19th century through the 20th century, reflecting the development
and cultural history of the city.

This section reviews Inglewood’s historical background, existing policies regarding historic
resources, and properties listed as historic resources and discusses the implications for historic
resources policy moving forward.

2.1 Historic Background
2.1.1 Native American History
In the prehistorical period, the coastal plain between present-day Los Angeles and Long Beach
was home to the Tongva people, also referred as the Gabrieleño, Fernandeño, or Nicoleño, the
names given to the region’s indigenous people by California’s Spanish missionaries. The Tongva
occupied the area now encompassed by the Los Angeles basin, San Fernando Valley, San Gabriel
Valley, San Bernardino Valley, and the local California coastline. The South Bay region was home
to a number of small Tongva villages, with notable settlements at Suangna near the present-day
city of Carson, near Point Fermin in San Pedro, and near Malaga Cove in Palos Verdes.1

2.1.2 Spanish Colonial and Mexican Periods
In 1542, Spanish explorer Juan Rodriguez Cabrillo led the first European expedition to explore
what is now the west coast of North America. Explorers with Cabrillo’s expedition encountered
native people on land and sea voyages, making what is thought to be the first known contact with
Alta California’s indigenous tribes, including the Tongva of the Suangna area. 2 Though Cabrillo
claimed California for the Spanish Crown at this time, Spanish settlement would not reach this
territory for another two hundred years.

On July 14, 1769, Don Gaspar de Portolá, governor and military leader of Baja California, led the
first expedition to colonize Alta California. Accompanied by Franciscan friars Junípero Serra and
Juan Crespí, Portolá took a group of 64 men northward from San Diego toward Monterey. On
August 2nd the expedition camped along the east bank of the Los Angeles River just south of
where it is joined by the Arroyo Seco. Fr. Crespí named the spot El Pueblo de Nuestra Señora la
Reina de los Ángeles del Río Porciúncula (i.e., Town of Our Lady the Queen of Angels of the River
Porciúncula). When the expedition crossed the river and continued to the south and west for
about a mile, they encountered the Tongva village of Yang-na, believed to be near the current
site of El Pueblo de Los Angeles.

On September 8, 1771, Spanish colonists established Mission San Gabriel, the fourth of what
would eventually be twenty-one Spanish missions in California, and the first in this area. Much of
the area’s native population would work the San Gabriel Mission lands. Seven years later, in 1778,
Governor Felipe de Neve received approval for the creation of a civil pueblo along the Río la
Porciúncula. Persuaded by Crespi’s earlier descriptions of a well-watered valley with good soils for
growing crops, the Spanish colonial government ordered Governor Neve to establish a settlement
at this location and name the new pueblo La Reina de los Angeles (“Queen of the Angels”).

In 1821, Mexico won its independence from Spain, and Alta California became a territory of the
new Mexican Republic, marking an end to Spanish colonial rule in the region. The political and
social control of the military and religious leadership began to shift toward the secular and private
sector. The Mexican government sought to diminish the influence of Spain in the region but the
missions largely remained loyal to the Roman Catholic Church in Spain. At the same time, there
was a need for more grazing lands to increase commerce in the hide and tallow trade. Thus,
beginning in 1834, the Mexican government began to secularize the missions, confiscating
mission lands to be distributed in large land grants called ranchos. Pío Pico, the last governor of
Alta California, subdivided the former mission lands into large tracts, granting them to various
prominent Californios. 3

2.1.3 Early American Period
United States troops began occupying Alta California in 1846 at the advent of the Mexican
American War and soon gained possession of Los Angeles itself. However, Alta California would
not officially come under American rule until February 2, 1848, with the signing of the Treaty of
Guadalupe Hidalgo, which ceded the California territory to the United States and ended the war.
Importantly, the treaty provided that the existing land grants would be honored.

The origin of today’s City of Inglewood dates back to the mid-1800s and a dispute between two
prominent Californio families: the Ávilas and the Machados. José Manuel Orchado Machado was
a Spanish soldier who found the area around the Centinela Springs to be excellent grazing lands
and settled there in 1781. 4 In 1834, Machado’s son Ygnacio built the Centinela Adobe. 5 During

council in 1837, which gave official title of the area around Centinela Springs to the Machado
family as the 2,219-acre Rancho Aguaje de la Centinela. The Ávila family was granted the much
larger Rancho Sausal Redondo. At 22,458 acres, this land encompassed much of what is now the

Ultimately the Ávila family would lose both of the ranchos. Bruno Ávila lost Rancho Aguaje de la
Centinela through foreclosure in 1857; the property was subsequently acquired by Scotsman Sir
Robert Burnett in 1860. In 1868, the heirs of Antonio Ávila were forced to sell Rancho Sausal
Redondo to pay probate costs, and it was also acquired by Burnett. By 1872, Burnett combined
the total area of some 25,000 acres into the Centinela Ranch, thus reuniting the extent of the
original land grant. This ranch included what would ultimately become the coastal communities
of Playa del Rey, El Segundo, Manhattan Beach, Hermosa Beach, and Redondo Beach as well as
the inland communities of Westchester, Inglewood, Hawthorne, and Lawndale.

In 1873, Burnett returned to his native Scotland, leasing the combined rancho lands to Canadian
attorney Daniel Freeman and his wife, Catherine, with an agreement that they could eventually
purchase the property outright. 6 The Freeman family moved to the ranch, which Burnett had been
using to graze sheep and cattle. Daniel Freeman continued to graze the stock and started farming.
Ultimately Freeman would amass a fortune growing barley, olives, citrus fruits, and almonds. He
named his ranch “Inglewood,” after his birthplace in Ontario.

Following Catherine’s death, Daniel Freeman began to pursue the commercial development of his
expansive holdings. He first established the Centinela Land Company, which proved unsuccessful.
Then in 1887, as the California Central Railway laid tracks to Redondo Beach, Freeman sold some
11,000 acres of his ranch to the Centinela-Inglewood Land Company, which would subdivide the
acres into small parcels for the settlement of the new town of Inglewood. 7

In 1888, Freeman began work on an estate for himself and his family, with bricks provided by his
own newly established Continuous Brick Kiln Company of Inglewood and lumber from the recently
acquired local lumber mill. 8 In 1889, he built the Land Company office next to the train depot,
moving it to the grounds of his estate in 1895 where it served as his office until his death in 1918. 9
Ultimately, all 25,000 acres of the Centinela Ranch would be subdivided and developed; the only
remaining portion of the ranch is the one-acre site on which the Centinela Adobe sits.

2.1.4 Inglewood Townsite
The townsite of Inglewood was platted by the Centinela-Inglewood Land Company in 1888, by
which time the town already had a population of 300. 10 The plan divided the town into northern
and southern sections on either side of the newly completed Inglewood Division of the California
Central Railroad line—a subsidiary of the Atchison Topeka & Santa Fe Railway—that ran along
Florence Boulevard as it made its way from Los Angeles to Redondo Beach. The major north-south
street leading into Inglewood was Grevillea Avenue. Development during this period was sparse,
and most buildings were of impermanent wood-frame construction. The first few business
buildings clustered on narrow uniform lots along Grevillea Avenue and Commercial Street (now
La Brea Avenue) between Regent and Queen streets.

By 1892, the town of Inglewood was home to several small businesses, including a grocery, a post
office, a barber, a restaurant, and a large two-story hotel on Queen Street between Commercial
and Market. 11 At this time, Inglewood also had a post office, a railroad depot, and a large grain-
storage building along the Redondo Branch of the AT&SF railroad, as well as a handful of single-
family residences. Market Street was predominantly residential during this period; the opening of
a streetcar line along its length in 1904 would lead to its gradual transition to a commercial
corridor.

By 1907, downtown Inglewood had several dozen dwellings. Commercial establishments included
a drug store, general merchandise store, grocery, meat market, tailor, print shop, and various
lodging buildings and offices. Institutional properties included a public school and a Presbyterian
church. Industrial uses were clustered along the rail lines and included a greenhouse, planning
mill, lumber yard, cement storage, gain mills and storage, and several warehouses.12

In 1905, a group of local businessmen formed the Inglewood Park Cemetery Association, acquiring
a large plot of land just east of what would become downtown Inglewood. In the cemetery’s first
year of operation, 32 internments took place, with funerals often arriving by rail from Los Angeles
in a private funeral car. 13 In 1907, the cemetery erected the Romanesque-style Grace Chapel, a
three-quarters replica of a church in Edinburgh, Scotland. Within a decade, the cemetery erected
the Neoclassical-style Inglewood Mausoleum, the first community mausoleum in the State of
California. 14 Many of the South Bay region’s earliest settlers have been laid to rest at Inglewood
Park Cemetery, including a number of Civil War veterans. 15 Other notable residents include former
Los Angeles Mayor Tom Bradley, Chet Baker, Ray Charles, Ella Fitzgerald, Etta James, boxer Sugar
Ray Robinson, and architect Paul Williams. 16

The City of Inglewood was officially incorporated on February 14, 1908.

2.1.5 City of Inglewood
By 1912, Inglewood’s commercial core was beginning to take shape along Commercial Street
between Los Angeles Street/Inglewood Avenue (now Florence Avenue) and Queen Street. Deep,
narrow lots were developed with various commercial uses. Market Street remained primarily
residential during this period, with a few commercial buildings and a Methodist church. 17

By 1920, the South Bay’s local economy was booming due to the region’s fertile agricultural lands,
productive oil fields, and emerging aviation industry. The City of Inglewood was growing
exponentially, with hundreds of new homes being built and the city’s commercial development
coalescing into a downtown business district along Commercial Street between Regent and
Queen Streets. 18

Inglewood had a number of churches by this time, including the First Methodist Episcopal Church,
St. John’s Catholic Church, Church of the Brethren, and Christian Church. 19 The only church that
survives from this period is Holy Faith Episcopal Church at the southeast corner of Locust Street
and Grace Avenue. 20 The church was first established in 1911, with services held in the Inglewood
Masonic Hall. In 1912, Grace Freeman Howland 21 and her husband Charles donated the funds to
erect a religious complex consisting of a church, a rectory (the dwelling to the south), and parish
hall (now a school at the rear). They hired a young architect, Philip Frohman, to design what would
be hailed as “the most perfect example of true Gothic architecture in the West.” The church was

On the evening of June 21, 1920, the Los Angeles Basin was rattled by an estimated 5.0 earthquake
centered near Inglewood. Tremors were felt as far away as Ventura and Riverside, but most of the
damage was in Inglewood, specifically, to the unreinforced brick buildings along Commercial
Street (now La Brea Avenue), where exterior walls fell into the street and plate glass windows
shattered. 23 The Inglewood Hotel was also badly damaged and subsequently demolished. Despite
the widespread damage, however, the earthquake did not seriously hamper the city’s growth. The
1920 census credited Inglewood with a population of 3,286. In just two years the figure would
double, making Inglewood the fastest growing city in the nation. 24 It was at this time that single-
family residential neighborhoods began to expand outward from central Inglewood.

The 1920s was a period of enormous growth for Inglewood, both in terms of population and
development. Though Commercial Street continued to be the primary artery of the downtown
business district, many more businesses were being established on Market Street and its cross-
streets during this period. At least seven new buildings were constructed in the 100 block of North
Market Street alone. The local financial institution, the People’s Federal Building & Loan
Association, was established at this time, first in a unit of the building at 314 S. Market Street,
before constructing its own building at the northeast corner of Market Street and Pimiento Street
(now Manchester Boulevard) in 1927. 25 That same year, the Bank of Inglewood erected a two-
story mixed-use building at the northeast corner of Market and Queen streets at a cost of
$140,000. Designed by local architect William L. Campbell in the Mediterranean Revival style, the
reinforced concrete building was touted as the “first steel frame business block in this city” and as
“practically fire and earthquake proof.” 26

the opening of a new ornamental lighting system installed along Market Street. In addition to
providing much needed illumination, the standards also supported the trolley wires of the Los

Toward the end of the 1930s, Inglewood’s economic base began to expand outside the downtown
core. Appropriately, in 1937 Commercial Street was officially changed to La Brea Avenue,
connecting it with the street in Los Angeles. 29 Also that year, Mines Field, which had been
established just southwest of the city, was purchased by the City of Los Angeles to serve as its

Hollywood Park brought in celebrated personalities associated with the entertainment industry—
from studio executives Jack Warner, Walt Disney, and Samuel Goldwyn, to A-list performers like
Al Jolson and Bing Crosby—many of whom were also investors in the operation.

2.1.6 Wartime and Postwar Growth
As war clouds gathered in the early 1940s, a number of aviation-related and other wartime
manufacturing facilities set up shop around the Los Angeles Airport. North American Aviation, Inc.
and the Northrup Company both established airplane manufacturing plants in the vicinity. Due to
the emergence of these new facilities, this area would not only be critical to the defense industry
during World War II, but in the postwar years would evolve into one of the most important centers
of the nation’s aerospace industry.

The presence of wartime and postwar manufacturing jobs added sharply to the local population
and financially supported a growing middle class throughout the South Bay region, including in
Inglewood. In 1938, the city had a population of 26,000; by 1956, that number had grown to
64,000. 31 Housing construction naturally responded to the increased demand, and commercial
development followed, leading to a pattern of postwar decentralization. By the mid-1950s, the
city had three retail business areas—in North Inglewood, Morningside Park, and Crenshaw—in
addition to the downtown.

The Fox Theater opened on March 31, 1949, on Market Street between Regent and Queen. Erected
on the site of the Granada Theater, which burned down in 1945, it was the last theater constructed
by the Fox West Coast Theater chain. Designed by prolific theater architect S. Charles Lee in the
Late Moderne style, it was the first theater in Inglewood to have air conditioning. Other features
included automatic lobby doors, CinemaScope widescreen projections, assistance for the hearing
impaired, and a soundproof “crying room.” The Fox Inglewood was often used for Fox Pictures’
premiers and sneak previews. 32

In the late 1950s pioneering Black families first began purchasing homes in Inglewood and the
immediately surrounding communities. These families were often met by racial intimidation from
their White neighbors. Prior to this, Black people had been effectively excluded from residing in
Inglewood, which had a well-earned reputation for racial discrimination. The 1960 census counted
just 29 Black residents in Inglewood out of 63,390 residents total, and no Black children attended
Inglewood schools. 33 In 1970, a group of parents successfully sued the Inglewood School District,
accusing it of discriminating against Blacks and other minority children. A Los Angeles Superior
Court judge agreed and imposed a mandatory integration plan, resulting in massive cross‐town
busing. School integration in Inglewood proved to be difficult and often violent; many White
families rapidly pulled their children out, sold their homes, and relocated outside of Inglewood. 34

By 1975, the level of Black and other non-White students in Inglewood had risen from 38 percent
to 80 percent, and the courts permitted Inglewood to drop its desegregation plan.35

As was true in most downtown areas during the postwar years, the primacy of the city’s downtown
as a commercial district was substantially diminished by increased competition from outlying
commercial areas. The removal of the Market Street trolley line in 1957 added further stress to
already struggling businesses. The City responded by adding municipally owned off-street parking
lots located throughout the district to draw car-dependent shoppers. The Chamber of Commerce
and Downtown Inglewood Retail Merchants Association coordinated to organize various
promotional activities as well as physical improvements like tree planting in the center strip and
along sidewalks, which were in place by the early 1960s. 36 However, the effects of these efforts
were soon eclipsed by the continued loss of customers to new shopping malls in communities
throughout Los Angeles. Inglewood considered, but ultimately rejected plans to build a mall of its
own on a large parcel at Prairie and Manchester, a proposal largely defeated by the Market Street
merchants. The site would instead become the home of the Forum. 37

In the late 1960s, nationally prominent businessman Jack Kent Cooke selected the site of a former
golf course at the southeast corner of Prairie Avenue and Manchester Boulevard to erect a new
venue for his three professional sports franchises: the Los Angeles Lakers NBA basketball team,
the Los Angeles Kings NHL hockey team, and the short-lived Los Angeles Wolves professional
soccer team. The Forum, a multipurpose indoor arena, was designed by the prominent Los
Angeles architectural firm Charles Luckman & Associates and completed in 1967. 38 Designed in
the New Formalist architectural style, it was intended as a modern and highly stylized version of
the Coliseum of ancient Rome. Nicknamed “the Fabulous Forum,” it would host tennis matches,
boxing matches, ice shows, rodeos, the circus, award shows, and political events. In 1972, the
Forum was the site of the Lakers’ first NBA championship since moving to Los Angeles; five
additional titles would follow in the 1980s. From the mid-1970s through the 1990s, the Forum
would serve as the premier large-scale concert venue for the Los Angeles area and would be
influential in the birth of “arena rock.” During the 1984 Olympics, the Forum was the venue for
men’s and women’s basketball. 39

By the early 1970s, shoppers had largely abandoned the downtown business center for suburban
malls, and key downtown tenants like J.C. Penney closed their doors. In an effort to reinvigorate
the core of the city, from 1971 to 1976 Inglewood spent about $50 million in local, county, and
federal funds to erect a new civic center complex along La Brea Avenue, just one block west of
downtown. This new complex, designed by Charles Luckman & Associates combined city hall, a
courthouse, library, fire and police facilities, public health complex, and a major new parking
garage on a single superblock, surrounded by expanses of lawn and public art. As hoped, this new
construction sparked a flurry of new commercial development in the larger In-Town
Redevelopment Area 40—bounded by Florence, Locust, Manchester and Fir—the vast majority of
which was office space and not retail. Several residential projects were built at this time as well,
most notably the 200-unit Inglewood Meadows housing complex on Locust Street, just east of
downtown. 41

While these projects brought large numbers of people into the vicinity of Market Street, their
presence did not raise the corridor’s fortunes, and the vitality of the downtown business district
continued to wane into the 1980s. Yet another sign of downtown’s economic decline, the Fox
Theater, then owned by the Mann theater chain, closed its doors in 1988.

Since the late 1970s, at least four City-sponsored revitalization programs have focused on
improving Market Street’s commercial viability, introducing street landscaping and furniture as
well as façade improvements to the existing buildings. Efforts have included a façade
improvement program designed by architectural firm Kahn, Kappe, Lotery, Boccato (1979); a
$250,000 façade improvement program, including signs and awnings (1984); a California Main
Street Community Project (1990s); and the Market Street Renaissance program (2000). However,
despite these efforts, Market Street has largely remained an underutilized asset.

2.1.7 Inglewood Today
In 1994, Hollywood Park underwent a $100 million expansion and became the Hollywood Park
Casino. This extended the facility’s economic viability until 2013, when the Hollywood Park
racetrack closed at the end of the fall racing season. In 2015, the Inglewood City Council approved
a plan to build a 70,000-seat football stadium on the site in anticipation of the St. Louis Rams
moving back to Los Angeles.

The Forum remained the home of the Lakers and Kings until 1999, when both teams relocated to
the newly constructed Staples Center in downtown Los Angeles. Beginning in 2012, the Forum
underwent a substantial renovation, reopening in 2014. Later that year, the Forum was listed in
the National Register of Historic Places. The venue is inextricably tied to the identity of the City of
Inglewood, which adopted the moniker “City of Champions.” The Forum is slated to host the
gymnastics events for the 2028 Summer Olympics.

On January 12, 2016, the NFL voted to move the St. Louis Rams back to Los Angeles, with the San
Diego Chargers to follow. In October 2016, the last part of the former Hollywood Park racetrack,
the Casino, was demolished, and a new Hollywood Park Casino was opened next door. The casino
was the first development in the “Hollywood Park” district, a master-planned mixed-use district
with sports and entertainment venues, commercial development, housing, and parks.

The Los Angeles Stadium at Hollywood Park (SoFi Stadium) was constructed in 2020 and hosted
Super Bowl LVI in 2022 and the College Football National Championship in 2023, and will host the
opening and closing ceremonies and soccer events for the 2028 Summer Olympics.

More recently, a new sports and entertainment arena—the “Intuit Dome”—was constructed in
2024 and will serve as the new home of the LA Clippers and will also host live concerts and events.
The sports arena and entertainment venue is touted to be one of the most technologically
advanced in the world.

2.2 Listed Historic Resources in Inglewood
Several properties in Inglewood have been listed under federal and State designation programs
through the efforts of local advocacy groups, private property owners, or as a by-product of
federal environmental review. These include properties listed in the National Register of Historic
Places (NRHP) or properties formally determined eligible for listing in NRHP. Properties listed in
or formally determined eligible for listing in the NRHP are automatically listed in the California
Register of Historical Resources (CRHR). As such, these properties are considered historical
resources as defined by the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA).

To be listed in or eligible for listing in the NRHP, a resource must possess significance in American
history and culture, architecture, or archaeology. In addition, properties must also possess historic
integrity. According to National Park Service guidance, a property that is more than 50 years of
age can be considered for listing in the NRHP. Fifty years is a general estimate of time needed to
develop historical perspective and therefore to evaluate historic significance. 42

Listing in the NRHP is primarily honorary and does not in and of itself provide protection to a
historical resource. The primary effect of listing in the NRHP on private owners of historic buildings
is the availability of financial and tax incentives. For projects that receive federal funding, a
clearance process must be completed in accordance with Section 106 of the National Historic
Preservation Act. Furthermore, state and local regulations may apply to properties listed in the
NRHP.

The CRHR is an authoritative guide in California used by State and local agencies, private groups,
and citizens to identify the State's historical resources and to indicate what properties are to be
protected, to the extent prudent and feasible, from substantial adverse change to their
significance. 43 The criteria for listing in the CRHR are based on NRHP criteria. Guidance for
applying the CRHR criteria does not provide a specific age threshold for eligibility. However, it
does state that “sufficient time must have passed to obtain a scholarly perspective on the events
or individuals associated with the resource.” 44

2.3 Historic Resources Policy in Inglewood
2.3.1 Local Designation
The City of Inglewood does not have a historic preservation ordinance and does not maintain a
local designation program or official inventory of historic resources.

2.3.2 Cultural Education
The City of Inglewood maintains a public art education program that, in addition to public art,
includes information on local architecture and cultural history. The Inglewood Public Art website
provides self-guided tours under various cultural topics and an interactive map in addition to
lesson plans and presentations. 45 These materials highlight several properties that are important
for their architectural merit. These include the Inglewood Post Office (1937) at 300 E. Hilcrest
Avenue; three Modernist single-family homes (1939) designed by master architect Rudolph
Schindler at 423, 429, and 433 W. Ellis Avenue; and the former Academy Theater (1939) designed
by noted theater architect Charles S. Lee at 3141 Manchester Boulevard. An example of “Googie”
commercial architecture, the Cafetales Restaurant (1957) at 115 S. La Brea Avenue, is highlighted,
as is the former “Brolly Hut” restaurant (1968) at 11205 Crenshaw Boulevard, a notable example
of Programmatic architecture. Photographs of these properties are provided below and their
locations are noted on Figure 2-2.

2.4 Findings
2.4.1 Key Findings
1. Human occupation and settlement on what is today the City of Inglewood has been
  documented to pre-colonial times and encompasses diverse and wide-ranging historic
  narratives. The existing built environment includes properties dating back to the 19th century
  and all decades of the 20th century.

2. Several buildings and sites have been listed under national and state programs through the
  efforts of private property owners or through federal environmental review processes.

3. The City of Inglewood lacks a historic preservation ordinance and does not maintain a local
  designation program or inventory of historic resources.

4. Many properties are understood to be culturally important through public awareness and
  education efforts by the City and nonprofit organizations. However, the historic significance
  of these properties and/or their eligibility for listing as historic resources has not necessarily
  been officially determined or recognized.

2.4.2 Policy Implications
1. The small number of properties in Inglewood that have been listed as historic resources were
  recognized under federal and State programs through the efforts of private property owners
  or through federal environmental review processes. In the absence of a local ordinance,
  preservation efforts may be inconsistent and dependent on the specific circumstances of each
  case, leading to uneven treatment of historic resources across the city.

2. Properties in Inglewood can be and are identified as eligible for historic listing through
  environmental review under CEQA. These findings, however, are typically only meaningful for
  analytical purposes of the project for which the findings were made and do not constitute
  long-term recognition of historic significance.

2.4.3 Opportunities and Constraints
1. City policy regarding historic resources can create more certainty for property owners,
  developers, and preservationists about the local rules and regulations governing historic
  resources and help avoid disputes and inconsistent outcomes.

2. Increased recognition and protection of the city’s significant historical, cultural, and
  architectural heritage can greatly enhance community identity, fostering a unique sense of
  place that resonates with residents and visitors. By celebrating and preserving historic
  resources, the City not only strengthens its local character but also engages visitors with its
  rich history. Additionally, such efforts contribute to historic education, allowing people to
  engage with and learn from the past, thereby deepening their connection to the community.

3. A local preservation program can make financial support available to aid in the restoration
  and maintenance of historic properties through preservation grants, tax incentives, and

4. Ultimately, the decision to implement or forgo a City preservation program should be rooted
  in a comprehensive evaluation of the City's long-term goals, the values held by the community,
  and the historical significance of its landmarks. This careful consideration ensures that any
  action taken aligns with the aspirations of residents while honoring the cultural heritage that
  defines the city's unique identity.

opened Metro K Line servicing South Los Angeles and Inglewood, and the planned Inglewood
Transit Connector project (an elevated people-mover that will connect the Hollywood Park/sports-
entertainment complex with the Downtown Inglewood K Line station), can assist with reducing
congestion and improving air quality. Alternatively, the City may consider adding more jobs in the
sectors where residents are currently leaving the city to find employment, such as educational
services; administration and support; and professional, scientific, and technical services. Doing so
would decrease job outmigration, reducing vehicle miles traveled among residents and ultimately
lowering greenhouse gas emissions.

3.3 City General Fund Revenues
This section observes key trends in Inglewood’s General Fund tax revenues with a particular focus
on property tax, sales and use tax, and TOT revenues. Sales tax revenues and growth patterns
between the City subtotal and the City’s share of the Los Angeles County Pool (“County Pool”) are
also identified. Additionally, this section examines retail sales by retail category to observe the
largest sales tax generators in the city.

It is important to note the differences between sales taxes and use taxes and how each is recorded.
Retail sales are subject to sales taxes if the sale occurs at a place of business in California that
participates in the sale and if the title (or ownership) to the goods passes to a customer. For
example, if a business has a storefront in Inglewood and sells a product to a customer, sales tax
is collected from that sale. The City’s portion of that sales tax revenue is observed in the following
data as part of the City subtotal.

If either of the aforementioned conditions of a sale are not met, use tax is applied to the sale. Use
tax is applied to the sales price of goods that were purchased from a retailer and are stored, used,
and consumed in the state. Local use tax is allocated to municipalities via the County Pool. Each
city within a county receives a prorated amount of the revenues collected in the County Pool
based on the proportion of local tax that is directly allocated to cities within their respective
county. For example, if an online retailer received an order and ships an item from out of state to
a resident in Inglewood, use tax would be applied. When the retailer files a sales and use tax
return, that sale would be allocated through the County Pool, and Inglewood would later receive
a prorated amount of revenues.

3.3.1 General Fund Revenues
In FY 2021-2022, the City received 29 percent of its General Fund revenues from property tax,
14 percent from sales and use tax, and 4 percent from TOT. When observing all cities in California,
approximately 39 percent of general fund revenues were generated from property tax, 22 percent
from sales and use tax, and 6 percent from TOT. Figure 3-9 shows a breakdown of the general
fund tax revenues by category for the City compared to California cities in FY 2021-2022.

  3.3.2 Sales and Use Tax and TOT
  Sales and Use Tax

  Inglewood’s sales tax rate is 10.00 percent, slightly higher than Los Angeles County (9.5 percent).
  The State of California levies 7.25 percent (1 percent of which goes to the City in the form of a

  an additional 2.25 percent district sales tax is imposed by the County, and the City imposes an
  additional 0.5 percent sales tax (also a form of district sales tax). The extra 0.5 percent imposed by
  Inglewood began in 2006 with the passage of Measure IT, a half-cent sales tax measure for public
  safety and law enforcement purposes.

Transient Occupancy Tax

TOT experienced a 41 percent growth in revenue (nearly $2 million) in FY 2021-2022, well
exceeding pre-COVID-19 pandemic levels. Per Inglewood’s proposed budget FY 2023-2024, the
City anticipated TOT revenue to maintain at this level in FY 2022-2023 and FY 2023-2024. The City
currently imposes a 15.5 percent hotel tax rate on transients staying in the city. This rate recently
increased from the previous 14.0 percent following the passage of Measure H in 2021. The City
estimated that with the implementation of this measure, TOT would generate an estimated
$730,000 in general fund revenue annually. Although Measure H recently passed, Inglewood’s
TOT revenue has only averaged about 4 percent of General Fund revenues between 2018 and
2022. Comparatively, TOT revenue across all California cities was 6 percent during the same
period. TOT could be an area of potential revenue growth for the City, particularly given the
additional demand generated from the construction and opening of new sports/entertainment
venues, along with the city’s close proximity to LAX.

3.4 Visitation Trends
Placer.ai is a mobile data analytics tool that tracks the movement of people across 500 different
mobile applications and measures foot traffic patterns among visitors, residents, and employees.
For the following analysis, Placer.ai was used to measure visitation trends to and from the city by
both visitors and employees.

3.4.1 Visitor and Employee Trends in the City of Inglewood
Inglewood hosts several sports and entertainment attractions year-round at several locations
within and in proximity to the Hollywood Park/sports-entertainment complex, including SoFi
Stadium (a 70,000-seat stadium, home to the National Football League’s Los Angeles Rams and
Los Angeles Chargers), the Intuit Dome (an 18,000-seat indoor arena, home to the National
Basketball League’s Los Angeles Clippers), the Kia Forum (a renovated 17,500-seat indoor arena,
formerly used for professional sports, now used as a concert/entertainment venue), and the
YouTube Theater, a 6,000-seat music and theater venue.

SoFi Stadium was the first major completed piece of the Hollywood Park/sports-entertainment
complex. It opened in September 2020 and has been a major catalyst for additional development
. This development, along with the subsequent construction of the YouTube Theater (2021), The
Shops at Hollywood Park (2022-2023), and Intuit Dome (2024) drive additional foot traffic to the
city. It is important to note that although the sports teams follow a seasonal schedule (September
to January for football and October to April for basketball), SoFi Stadium and Intuit Dome also
host various concerts and other attractions throughout the year.

Figure 3-12 shows monthly visitor and employee visits to the city from January 2020 to November
2023 compared to the same months from a baseline year (2019). We can see that during the
COVID-19 pandemic there was a sharp decline in visits by both visitors and employees in March
and April of 2020. The overall average monthly visits to the city in 2020 declined by 24 percent for
visitors and 20 percent for employees.

3.5 Findings
3.5.1 Community Outreach Feedback
One of the key categories examined in community and stakeholder outreach was the economy.
During the outreach sessions and surveys, feedback was solicited as to what people appreciate
about the city today, what is currently missing or needed in the city, things that need
improvement, and a vision for the city’s future.

What People Appreciate about the City

Commenters provided positive feedback about the new sports and entertainment venues,
increased property values, and the City’s improved fiscal standing. Comments also reflect an
appreciation for the city’s convenient shopping and iconic stores, including Randy’s Donuts.
Stakeholders like that the City provides opportunities for new and small businesses to establish
themselves and thrive, including Black-owned businesses. Commenters also appreciate the City’s
rent control program.

What Is Missing or More Is Needed

Commenters have expressed a strong desire for more grocery stores, especially high-end and
organic options like Trader Joe's, Whole Foods, Sprouts, and Erewhon, because of concerns over
existing supermarkets closing and limited current options. There's a significant call for improved
dining and retail experiences, including upscale restaurants that could benefit from event
attendance, and a variety of eateries like fine dining and nonchain diners. Specific restaurant
suggestions include Joey's, Cava, Javier's, and Mastro's, along with interest in attracting retail
stores like Nike and Walmart to enhance shopping options.

Revitalization of Market Street is a key priority, with commenters nostalgic about its historical role
and future potential. Suggestions include fixing up the area, capitalizing on its "good bones," and
possibly establishing a Business Improvement District (BID). Economic development and job
opportunities are also highlighted, with a need for more jobs and workforce training programs.
Residents advocate for partnerships with industries to create high-paying jobs, including
establishing a business incubator and programs to help the homeless gain employment.

Investment in education is important because of concerns about low-performing schools amid
high mortgage costs. Commenters desire investment in educational programs like language
immersion and STEM, and call for more schools to improve educational outcomes. Housing
affordability and the overall cost of living are major concerns, with multiple mentions of the need
to lower rent and reduce property taxes. Additionally, there's a desire for enhanced community
amenities like more tree services, water parks, affordable recreational facilities, and affordable
entertainment options such as movie theaters with lower ticket prices and parking fees.

Page 3-32  CITY OF INGLEWOOD | EXISTING CONDITIONS REPORT | January 2025
   Chapter 3 Demographic Economic Profile

What Needs to Improve

Stakeholders have expressed significant concerns about issues they feel need improvement or are
not working well in the city. Affordable housing and rising living costs top the list, with high rents
and property taxes making it increasingly difficult for residents to afford living in the area. There's
a strong call for more affordable housing options, stricter rent control policies, and measures to
prevent displacement, especially for long-term residents who feel they are being pushed out.

Support for small and local businesses is another major theme. Commenters highlight the need
for affordable commercial spaces, particularly on Market Street, to support small business
startups. Barriers such as rising costs, red tape, and stringent codes make it difficult for small
businesses to start and thrive. There's a desire for more business grants, incubators, and training
programs to foster entrepreneurship, especially among minority-owned and Black/Brown-owned
businesses.

Economic development and job opportunities are important, with calls for more jobs and better
employment prospects. Stakeholders suggest integrating the regional economy with the local
community and leveraging arts and culture as catalysts for economic activity. However, concerns
exist that the City’s infrastructure and services are not keeping pace with new developments,
leading to traffic congestion and parking shortages. There's also a sense that residents are not
benefiting from large-scale investments.

Visions for the City
Stakeholders envision Inglewood as a thriving, inclusive community that balances entertainment
with local needs. They seek economic development supporting small and minority-owned
businesses through grants and incentives and aim to attract upscale retailers and restaurants like
Trader Joe's and popular dining establishments to enhance local amenities.

Revitalizing Market Street into a cultural and entertainment hub with public art, museums, and
cultural centers is a priority, along with improved infrastructure for accessibility. Affordable
housing is a significant concern, with calls to prevent displacement and help renters become
homeowners to foster generational wealth. Residents want the city to prioritize their needs over
big corporations, ensuring venues like the So-Fi Stadium contribute fairly to the community.

Enhancing tourism amenities—such as hotels, outdoor dining, and retail stores—is welcomed if
aligned with community interests. There is a strong desire for better schools, more green spaces,
and job training programs for youth not pursuing college. Safety improvements, including hiring
more police officers and addressing social issues, were highlighted as important components of
a secure environment.

Overall, the vision is for Inglewood to support entrepreneurship and multi-generational living,
value long-term residents, preserve local culture, and enable businesses and the community to
thrive together.

3.5.2 Implications for Planning
The demographic findings in Inglewood provide key insights into the city’s evolving population,
housing trends, and economic landscape, all of which carry important implications for future city
planning. As Inglewood continues to experience changes in population composition, household
size, and employment patterns, City planners must consider strategic approaches to housing
affordability, economic development, and transportation infrastructure. These factors will shape
the City's ability to meet and support future demands for its diverse population and ultimately
foster sustainable growth. The following section outlines the most significant implications for city
planning based on these findings.

Housing Affordability and Development Needs. The slight decrease in population and decline
in household size suggest changing housing needs. The City must focus on fostering more
housing units to meet the Regional Housing Needs Assessment mandate of 7,439 new housing
units by 2029 and additional units throughout the horizon year of the General Plan. A significant
portion of these units must be affordable for low- and very-low-income residents, addressing
housing affordability challenges.

Economic Development and Employment Opportunities. There is significant job outmigration
in Inglewood, with many residents commuting outside the city for work because local jobs may
not align with residents’ abilities. This leads to economic leakage when earnings are spent
elsewhere. The main employment sectors include health care, retail, and hospitality, boosted by
developments like SoFi Stadium. To mitigate this, Inglewood should attract growth industries that
match the skills of its residents and enhance workforce programs that align training with local
industry needs. This approach can reduce job outmigration and stimulate local economic activity.

Education and Workforce Development. Educational attainment in Inglewood is below county
and state levels, limiting economic mobility and potentially contributing to the City’s lower
incomes, with 57 percent of households earning less than $75,000 annually. This impacts residents'
access to better jobs and may lead to residents seeking opportunities elsewhere. Investing in
education by improving K-12 resources and support, expanding higher education access through
partnerships with colleges, and offering vocational training aligned with industry needs can
enhance workforce development and economic prospects.

Retail and Commercial Development. Inglewood's residents and daytime population spend
approximately $855 million annually on key goods and services like groceries, dining,
transportation, and apparel. To capture more of this spending locally, the city can expand retail
and commercial offerings, supporting small businesses to keep money circulating within the
community and foster job creation. Developing mixed-use commercial areas that combine retail,
dining, entertainment, and residential spaces will attract foot traffic and enhance the city’s appeal.
Marketing Inglewood as a destination for shopping and entertainment can draw visitors from
surrounding areas, boosting economic activity and improving the overall quality of life.

  4 MARKET ANALYSIS
The Market Analysis begins by offering an overview of recent broader market trends, with
particular attention to how the COVID-19 pandemic has reshaped cities' approaches to various
land uses and market sectors. It then shifts focus to the City of Inglewood's notable growth and
development over the past five years, followed by a detailed examination of the retail, office,
industrial, multifamily, and hospitality sectors. Each market segment is analyzed through historical
trends, current vacancy rates, rent comparisons, and future outlooks, with comparisons drawn
between the City, the Inglewood Submarket, and Los Angeles County. The final part of this section
observes key land use findings from community/stakeholder outreach sessions, summarizes
market data, and provides demand estimates for the examined asset classes over the next 25
years. This section aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of market dynamics to guide
informed decision-making for future development.

4.1 Recent Market Trends
The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated existing trends and reshaped the way cities consider land
use. Key trends for each land use are outlined below.

•  Retail. Retail has been an ever-evolving asset class and changed significantly prior to (and
  following) the pandemic. The United States is significantly over-retailed (with over 23 square
  feet of shopping center space per capita). To adapt to the growing presence of online retailers
  and e-commerce, several brick-and-mortar retailers began reducing their physical footprint in
  favor of developing omni-channeling strategies to offer a seamless shopping experience to
  consumers via in-person or online modes of shopping. Additionally, as big-box anchors at
  shopping centers across the country began shutting, shopping center developers and owners
  reimagined many of these buildings from pure retail to a blend of uses, including residential
  and industrial.

  The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated these trends as people were quarantined at home and
  began relying on e-commerce and online retailers. For example, e-commerce sales in the
  United States increased by over 30% in Q2 2020, and e-commerce’s share of overall retail sales
  is expected to continue to increase in the near future (up to 25% of all retail sales within the
  next five years). Consumer online shopping behavior further solidified during the pandemic
  years and is unlikely to change, given rapid delivery options, including same-day delivery, by
  several e-commerce retailers. The types of retail that continue to grow and remain in demand
  include trip-generating uses, such as entertainment, experience, and essentials (e.g.,
  restaurants, bars, grocery).
•  Office. Office leasing activity dropped as remote work became the new normal during the
  COVID-19 pandemic. Research has shown that though work-from-home days have dropped
  from the pandemic high of 60%, employers expect an average of 2.3 work-from-home days
  per week, suggesting the hybrid home/office model is still being well-utilized post-pandemic.

  Telework and work-from-home options are reshaping the need for office space and business
  districts. Office space appears to be moving closer to suburban areas or is being integrated
  into more blended use environments (developments that include complementary land uses
  e.g., commercial, residential, hospitality).

•  Industrial/Flex. The merging of retail and industrial uses via e-commerce is accelerating the
  growth of industrial/flex uses. Last-mile delivery and sorting facilities are in high demand
  because e-commerce retailers cannot thrive without a significant distribution network.
  Additionally, flex space (space that is designed to be a versatile blend of industrial, office,
  research and development, incubator, tech, and retail-showroom) is a growing market. Cities
  like Inglewood may be able to attract high-tech firms and skilled workers with the ability to
  open such space.

•  Multifamily Residential. New housing can generate significant new tax revenues directly via
  annual property taxes and indirectly via sales tax revenues because remote workers can
  alleviate traffic and increase spending to support local businesses. Additionally, e-commerce
  spending from residents allows a greater proportion of County Pool revenues to be distributed
  to the City. Given this, housing does not necessarily have a net negative fiscal impact to a city,
  especially given rising property values for new construction. As work-from-home became the
  new normal, home office amenities are becoming increasingly important in both single family
  and multifamily residential projects. Lastly, as large retail centers are converting from pure
  retail centers to a blend of uses, we are beginning to see more residential uses in shopping
  centers.

•  Hospitality. The COVID-19 pandemic affected both business and leisure travel and thus
  significantly hurt the hospitality industry. However, as conferences and events are returning
  to in-person formats and leisure travel is rebounding, we are observing hotels approaching
  similar levels of occupancy as prior to the pandemic. Additionally, average daily rates (“ADR”)
  and revenue per available room (“RevPAR”) have increased gradually to offset the negative
  impacts of the pandemic.

4.2 Market Demand Analysis Overview
To better understand current market demand in the city, the project team utilized CoStar to
analyze and compare key market variables for various land uses—e.g., commercial (retail, office,
industrial/flex), residential, and hospitality (hotel)—across different geographies including the city
of Inglewood, the regional area bounded by Interstate (I-) 10, I-105, I-110, and I-405 (“Submarket,”
“Inglewood Submarket”) and Los Angeles County (see Figure 4-1).

The boundaries of the Inglewood Submarket were chosen for the following reasons. First, the top
three destinations where residents commute for work outside of Inglewood are Los Angeles, Santa
Monica, and Culver City, demonstrating that more residents commute to the north, west, and east
than make southbound commutes. Second, when observing a five-mile radius from Manchester
Blvd. and Prairie Ave., the radius captures most of the area bounded by I-10, I-105, I-110, and I-
405, along with portions of areas west of I-405 and south of I-105 (e.g., Hawthorne, Marina del
Rey, and El Segundo). If the areas west of I-405 and south of I-105 were included as part of the
Submarket, the data would skew toward a higher-end product and not be particularly
representative of the area surrounding Inglewood.

The Market Demand Analysis examined variables such as occupancy rates, market asking-rent
levels, construction trends, and overall inventory by Classes A, B, and C, as defined by CoStar. The
Analysis presents this data from a current snapshot (as of the end of the second quarter of 2024)
as well as a historical lens (from year-end 2013 to year-end 2023) to measure growth patterns
across these land uses in the City, Submarket, and Los Angeles County.

Per CoStar, a Class A building is a high-quality building that contains abundant amenities with a
proper maintenance and management team. These buildings typically have high-value tenants
and feature above-average rental rates. Conversely, Class B and Class C buildings feature fewer
amenities, typically offer lower rental rates, and may not have as prestigious a group of tenants
compared to a Class A building.

The findings from CoStar will inform near-term and long-term market demand estimates for the
examined land uses.

Current Snapshot: Vacancy Rates and Rent Comparisons

The City is currently facing higher vacancy rates in its retail market compared to both the
Submarket and the County. Inglewood's retail vacancy rate stands at 6.1%, notably higher than
