Future Retail Development

Retail dynamics are shifting due to a combination of store closures, bankruptcies, and the rise of
e-commerce. As a result, many retail centers are being transformed into a blend of uses that
integrate retail with other functions. Today, retail is increasingly anchored by "trip-generators" like
entertainment, experiential offerings, and essential services, such as food and groceries.

Looking forward, retail development in Inglewood is somewhat limited, consistent with broader
trends in the Submarket. Currently, only two retail buildings are under construction in the
Submarket, totaling 68,601 SF. Proposed projects include three retail buildings, one of which is
planned in Inglewood. This project is a smaller development consisting of a 2,000 SF Class B retail
pad at the southwest corner of Manchester Boulevard and Van Ness Avenue. Despite trends
suggesting reduced demand for traditional retail space in the city due to e-commerce growth,
there is still notable interest in new retail development. This demand is being driven by the
emergence of major sports and entertainment venues at the Hollywood Park/sports-
entertainment complex, which are expected to generate significant foot traffic, as well as the
housing developments designed to support these venues.

A significant portion of Inglewood's retail space is over 40 years old, accounting for 3.9 million SF,
or 63% of the total 6.1 million SF of retail space in the city. Concentrations of retail space older
than 40 years can be found primarily in the area bounded by I-405 to the west, Manchester Blvd.
to the north, Prairie Ave. to the east, and Imperial Hwy. to the south. Additional concentrations
can be found at the intersections of Crenshaw Blvd. and Imperial Hwy., Crenshaw and Manchester
Blvds., and along Centinela Ave. and Market St. / La Brea Ave. north of Manchester Blvd.

Of this older stock, approximately 20% (780,000 SF) has the potential to be reimagined either as
modern retail space or as retail space combined into a development with a blend of supporting
uses (e.g., residential/retail). This represents a key opportunity for revitalization, which could
transform older retail areas to better align with current market demands and the City’s growth
trajectory.

Given that Inglewood’s retail space currently faces higher vacancies and challenges with leasing
large developments like The Shops at Hollywood Park, there appears to be limited demand for
significantly more retail space to be built over the next 25 years, unless older retail space or vacant
land was replaced or reimagined into a mixed-use development with some retail uses along major
transit areas or, as the public desired, along corridors such as Century Blvd., Market St., and
Imperial Hwy. In these scenarios, approximately 5 to10 SF of local-serving retail/restaurants could
be added per new residential unit. Based on Regional Housing Needs Assessment (“RHNA”)
projections, the City is expected to show capacity to support 7,439 new housing units from 2021
to 2029 (~930 units per year). This would imply that the City could add 4,650 to 9,300 SF of retail
space per year or approximately 116,250 to 232,500 SF of retail over the next 25 years, including
the potential reimagining or replacing of older retail space. Efforts to modernize older retail stock
and encourage strategic new development could strengthen Inglewood’s position within the
regional retail market in the coming years.

Class A office space accounts for the largest portion of the market at 38%, with six buildings

work—offices were shut down and employees began working remotely. Office vacancy in the city
rose from 20.7% in 2019 to 26.1% by the end of 2023. The broader Inglewood Submarket
experienced a similar trend but with more dramatic increases; vacancy more than doubled from
8.4% in 2019 to 20.3% in 2023. Comparatively, vacancy rates in the County in the ten-year span
did not rise beyond 15.5%. Although Inglewood has overall higher levels of vacancy compared to
the surrounding Submarket, it is important to note that more than half of the vacant space in the
city can be attributed to three buildings, one of which is the aforementioned NFL Media Building.

Despite the rise in vacancies, office rents in Inglewood have steadily increased, growing by 43%
over the past decade, from $30.05 per SF in 2013 to $42.90 in 2023. This trend suggests that while
occupancy challenges persist, landlords have been able to maintain or even increase rental prices,
possibly due to the quality of space or specific market conditions. Comparatively, rents in the
broader Inglewood Submarket grew at a slightly slower rate of 35%, $35.72 per SF to $48.15,
reflecting less pressure on pricing in the Submarket. The difference in rent growth between

Future Office Development

Looking forward, several developments are in the proposal phase in Inglewood, but currently, no
office buildings are under construction. The City has three proposed buildings at Hollywood Park,
totaling 545,718 SF. These planned developments are significant but remain in early stages,
contributing to a lack of immediate growth in the office market. If they were to be built, however,
these buildings would add significant office space to the market.

In contrast, the broader Inglewood Submarket is experiencing more construction activity. Four
buildings are currently under construction, adding 332,413 SF, and 11 proposed developments
are in the pipeline (including the three in Inglewood’s Hollywood Park/sports-entertainment
complex), five in Culver City, and three in LA, totaling 2.22 million SF of office space. This suggests
that while Inglewood is preparing for growth, neighboring areas like Culver City and parts of Los
Angeles are more actively expanding their office markets. Given that more people are working
from home, in-home office type amenities will be important to consider for future development.

Approximately 82% of Inglewood’s office space is over 40 years old, totaling 2.85 million SF. Given
the limited demand for additional office space, it is anticipated that up to 20% of the older office
space, about 570,000 SF, has the potential to be reimagined or redeveloped as part of a mixed-
use commercial/residential development. A large portion of that space could be turned into a
higher-demand office use, such as medical office. This presents an opportunity to reposition older
properties to meet modern demands, potentially incorporating a blend of uses to attract tenants
and improve occupancy.

4.2.3 Industrial/Flex Market
E-commerce is accelerating growth of industrial use. Retail and industrial are merging, with space
being used for Buy Online Pick Up in Store, fulfillment, last-mile logistics, and warehousing
(including flex space such as research and development). This analysis compared key variables in
the industrial and flex space market (hereafter, “industrial market”) in the city, the Submarket, and
the County.

The industrial market in Inglewood encompasses a total of 5.5 million SF spread across 348
buildings. This market represents 44% of the industrial and flex space in the Submarket. The
industrial sector is primarily composed of Class B and Class C properties, with Class B buildings
accounting for 31% (67 buildings) and Class C buildings representing the majority at 65% (272
buildings). The city has only one Class A building, which comprises 0.3% of the industrial space.

The flex space market in the city includes 20 buildings totaling 203,000 SF and maintains a
relatively low vacancy rate of 5.0%. Meanwhile, the industrial-only portion of the city’s market
consists of 328 buildings with 5.3 million SF and a slightly higher vacancy rate of 5.6%. These
figures highlight the relative stability of the industrial sector, with only modest fluctuations in
vacancy.

activity in the Submarket occurred in Inglewood. In the ten-year span, six buildings totaling

Future Outlook
Despite the strong demand for industrial space driven by e-commerce, logistics, and last-mile
delivery needs, there are currently no new industrial or flex projects planned, proposed, or under
construction in Inglewood or the Submarket. This lack of future development may indicate
potential opportunities for the City to capitalize on emerging trends in warehouse and sorting
facilities as well as flex space for tech and medical industries by re-envisioning or redeveloping its
existing space. Further, Inglewood's strategic location near Los Angeles International Airport
(“LAX”) and the 405 and 105 Freeways may entice prospective developers and tenants.

Approximately 79% of Inglewood’s industrial and flex space is over 40 years old, totaling almost
4.3 million SF. Observing the last ten years of construction and demolition of industrial space, the
City saw a 200,000 SF net gain of industrial space, or 20,000 SF new space per year. Presuming
similar construction trends, growing demand for modern industrial facilities, and given most of
the industrial space in the Submarket is being absorbed by Inglewood, there is roughly 20,000 to
25,000 SF of industrial demand in the City per year (between 500,000 and 625,000 SF over 25
years). The replacement or redevelopment of older industrial buildings could encompass a
significant portion of future industrial space. This could include transforming outdated buildings
into more efficient warehouses, logistics hubs, or flex spaces that cater to the evolving demands
of e-commerce and other industries.

In Inglewood, the multifamily residential market plays a crucial role in meeting housing demand,
offering 12,934 units across 540 buildings. These units represent approximately 20% of the overall
multifamily market in the Inglewood Submarket. The city's multifamily stock provides a diverse
range of housing options, including market-rate, affordable, and senior units spread across Class
A, B, and C buildings, ensuring a variety of options for residents.

are more affordable compared to high-end Class A buildings. Net absorption in this segment (34

mid-tier properties given economic conditions and the cost of living in the broader region.

enters the market. Rent and vacancy data suggest that affordability remains a key concern for
residents. Inglewood’s future development should focus on keeping a diverse housing stock,
including preserving Class C properties and addressing the pressing need for more affordable
housing to sustain long-term growth and residential stability.

4.2.5 Hospitality Market
The COVID-19 pandemic dealt a severe blow to the global hospitality industry, and its effects were
clearly reflected in Inglewood's hotel market. The sector, particularly dependent on conventions,
business travel, and large-scale events, experienced unprecedented disruption due to travel
restrictions, social distancing mandates, and a sharp decline in both leisure and business travel.
Occupancy rates plummeted, ADR (Average Daily Rate) shrank, and RevPAR (Revenue per
Available Room) declined dramatically, pushing many hotels into financial distress.

To better understand the hospitality market, what must be first understood is the different classes
of hotels and how they correlate to service-type hotels. Hotels are categorized by class—economy,
midscale, upper midscale, upscale, upper upscale, and luxury. Limited-service hotels typically fall
under economy and midscale classes. These hotels are budget friendly, offering low-cost
accommodations and minimal amenities, and usually do not offer a full-service restaurant. Select-
service hotels offer more amenities than limited-service hotels, such as small meeting spaces, a
fitness center, and a casual restaurant. Select-service hotels are the fastest growing type of hotels
currently being developed and typically fall under upper midscale or upscale classes. Lastly, full-
service hotels offer a wider array of services, including larger banquet/conference spaces, multiple
restaurants and bars, shuttle services, expanded fitness centers, and spas. Full-service hotels may
refer to different hotel types, including boutique hotels and resorts, and generally fall within
upscale, upper upscale, and luxury classes.

Inglewood's hotel market is dominated by economy class hotels, most of which are independently
operated. The City’s hotel stock includes 45 operational hotels offering 2,309 rooms. Of these
rooms, 66.3% are economy, 27.2% are midscale, and 6.5% are upper midscale hotels. The bulk of
these hotels are in the southern part of the city along Century Boulevard and Imperial Highway,
servicing LAX. While Inglewood's hotels provide lower-cost options, the more upscale hotel
properties serving LAX are on the Los Angeles side, west of I-405. Figure 4-10 shows the location
of these hotels in the city. Inglewood accounts for 48% of the hotel rooms in the Submarket. There
are five hotels in the nearby unincorporated community of Lennox, adjacent to Inglewood in LA
County. Of these, four are economy-class independent hotels, collectively offering 112 rooms. The
fifth hotel is a 149-room upper midscale class Hampton Inn.

4.3 Findings
4.3.1 Community Outreach Feedback
One of the key categories examined in community and stakeholder outreach process was land
use. During the outreach sessions and surveys, feedback was solicited as to what people
appreciate about the city today, what is currently missing or needed in the city, things that need
improvement, and a vision for the city’s future. Below is a summary of those findings that relate
to the market categories described above.

Appreciate About the City

Commenters provided positive feedback about the City’s new sports and entertainment venues,
new developments, and increasing home values. Stakeholders expressed an appreciation for their
neighborhoods and the diversity of housing types present in the city. Commenters also like the
city’s proximity to amenities such as the beach and LAX.

January 2025 | CITY OF INGLEWOOD | EXISTING CONDITIONS REPORT  Page 4-33
 Chapter 4 Market Analysis

Missing / Need More of in the City

There is a significant emphasis on the need for more affordable housing, particularly housing for
seniors, low-income families, teachers, veterans, and Section 8 housing. Concerns about
homelessness and the need for long-term solutions for both short-term and long-term homeless
populations were highlighted as well.

Additionally, the desire for improved community amenities is evident, with suggestions for
facilities such as a skating rink, affordable gymnastics studios, and water parks. There is also
interest in creating more quality spaces for social interactions, such as sit-down restaurants, which
would enhance the quality of life for residents.

As far as retail is concerned, the community is particularly interested in adding higher-end grocery
options, such as Trader Joe’s and Whole Foods, along with healthy food options to further improve
the quality of life and the local shopping experience.

Need for Improvement

There is a strong call for improvements in the city’s infrastructure, with specific attention to
revitalizing Market Street, enhancing public spaces, and developing more community-centric
areas. Suggestions included the beautification of streets, mixed-use developments (e.g.,
residential and commercial), and creating more accessible community spaces that residents can
easily navigate without encountering significant traffic. Comments also suggest a demand for
more community services such as youth centers, public parks, and facilities like the YMCA. Such
enhancements to existing community spaces and better support for families and children were
seen as vital for strengthening the social fabric of the area.

Vision for the City

The community envisions a future where urban development is balanced with a focus on livability,
inclusivity, and sustainability. There is a strong desire to transform major streets like Century Blvd,
Imperial Hwy., and Market St. into areas with more mixed-use development and vibrant local
businesses that serve both residents and visitors. Revitalizing Downtown Inglewood to create a
thriving, pedestrian-friendly center filled with locally owned businesses is a core aspiration.

The community values preserving the character of their neighborhoods by promoting small-scale
urban farming, sustainable land use, and ensuring that development remains consistent with the
surrounding areas. Commenters also express a clear preference for preserving the integrity of
their neighborhood by capping building sizes and focusing on moderate growth that respects the
existing landscape.

4.3.2 Implications for Planning
The data in the Market Analysis section of the report demonstrates that the Hollywood
Park/sports-entertainment complex has driven significant construction in the area, including
320,000 square feet of retail, 451,000 square feet of office space, and 314 new rental housing
units.

While most of the new retail and office space added in the last ten years is at Hollywood Park,
another 881 housing units were added in the city within the last ten years (including 339 units in
2023). Additionally, 291,400 SF of industrial space were added in the city over the last ten years,
highlighting the growing demand for industrial uses. Despite the recent growth, there appears to
be limited commercial construction in the near future, with limited retail, office, and industrial
space in final planning and under construction. The asset classes exhibiting significant growth for
the future include multifamily residential and hospitality.

An additional 366 units will be added to the multifamily residential market in the city by 2026.
There are also approximately 2,300 additional units proposed in the city, many of which are
expected to be added to the Hollywood Park/sports-entertainment complex. From a hospitality
standpoint, there are currently three hotels varying from upper midscale to luxury class that will
add 624 new rooms to the city. These hotels are in or within close proximity to Hollywood Park.

Projects in the development pipeline, along with historical vacancies and population trends,
support future population growth in the City. Detailed summaries, along with demand projections
are observed for each asset class below.

Retail
The Shops at Hollywood Park added 320,000 SF of retail space to the Inglewood retail market but
it remains only 52% leased as of Q2 2024, driving higher vacancies. High vacancy and limited
construction in the pipeline indicate less demand for future retail construction. To backfill existing
space, the City could consider targeting retailers from categories that are exhibiting a retail sales
leakage in the city and are complementary to the Hollywood Park/sports-entertainment complex,
such as bars and pubs and full-service restaurants.

Based on stakeholder and community outreach feedback, there appears to be a strong desire for
mixed-use developments, including the blending of residential and retail uses. Using the existing
RHNA numbers, it is observed that the City needs to show capacity to build approximately 930
residential units per year. Given that in a mixed-use development, approximately 5 to 10 SF of
retail/restaurant space would be built per residential unit, it was calculated that the City could
potentially add between 4,650 and 9,300 SF of retail per year (or 116,250 to 232,500 SF over the
next 25 years). It is important to note that this additional retail space may include the replacement
or reimagination of existing retail space that is over 40 years old.

Lastly, community outreach findings also called for additional healthy and higher-end retail. As
more upscale developments are built in and around the Hollywood Park/sports-entertainment
complex, there could be potential to add such higher-end grocery options, such as a Trader Joe’s
or a Whole Foods.

Office

High office vacancy and lower office market rents compared to the Submarket and County along
with trends in the office market indicate less demand overall for future office space. Although the
City did add the 451,000 SF NFL Media Building in 2021, there has not been much else built in the
last 10 years, and there are no office buildings currently in final planning or under construction.

for approximately 20,000 to 25,000 SF of industrial space per year (or 500,000 to 625,000 SF over
the next 25 years). Since there is not much vacant land in the city, much of this demand will be
satisfied by reimagining or replacing existing industrial space that is over 40 years old.
Approximately 79% of existing industrial space is over 40 years old, and approximately 20% of
that space (860,000 SF) could be updated to accommodate the needs and demands of future
tenants.

Multifamily

The multifamily market in the city is strong and is growing significantly. Approximately, 1,195 units
were built in the last ten years (653 of which were in 2023 alone). There are two buildings currently
under construction that will add a combined 366 units by 2026. Additionally, there are another
approximately 2,300 units proposed in the city. If all of the proposed units are built, the City would
be well on its way to achieve its RHNA numbers. Higher density developments may provide a
balance for additional units and affordability.

The further buildout of the Hollywood Park/sports-entertainment complex, along with the
additional need for housing statewide and to meet residents’ desires for more housing,
particularly mixed-use developments with residential uses, it is anticipated that the share of future
housing growth in the Submarket will increase from 16% to nearly 50%. The growth rate of
housing production in the Submarket over the last 10 years was observed to be approximately
727 units per year. Going forward, the City could potentially add 350 to 400 units per year (or
between 8,750 and 10,000 units over the next 25 years). Ensuring proper mixed-use zoning in key
corridors throughout the city, such as Century Blvd., Imperial Hwy., and Market St., is critical to
meet that future demand.

Lastly, near-term population estimates were made based on housing units currently under
construction. Assuming a 5% vacancy rate across units currently under construction,

   Chapter 4 Market Analysis

approximately 348 units will be occupied. Per ESRI, the average household size in Inglewood has
slowly declined over the last 13 years and is expected to decline slightly in the next 5 years from
2.80 in 2023 to 2.76 in 2028. Applying the 2028 estimate, we can see that the 348 new units will
likely add 960 new residents to the city.

Hospitality
There have not been new hotels added in the city in last ten years, and hotel performance numbers
from existing hotels indicate that while ADR and RevPAR have increased, occupancy remains
below pre-pandemic levels. However, the venues at the Hollywood Park/sports-entertainment
complex draw a significant number of visitors and thus attract newer hotel development of a much
more upscale class than the city has seen in several decades. There are three hotels in final
planning, ranging from upper midscale to luxury class, and are expected to break ground within
a 12-month period. These hotels alone will add 624 new rooms to the market by early 2027.
Further hotel developments will continue to benefit being close to Hollywood Park as the city
becomes a top destination in the Los Angeles region for high-profile demand driving events.
Future development may likely shift towards higher-density and higher-class hotels along Century
Blvd. west of Prairie Ave. as older economy-class hotels get replaced. Such hotels would not only
service tourists, but business travelers arriving via LAX as well. Replacing older hotels will allow
Inglewood to be more competitive with hotels west of the city servicing LAX and capture more of
the growing leisure and business travelers associated with the new sports/entertainment facilities.

Near-term guest projections were made based on hotels currently in final planning. New hotel
development can be warranted when the market reaches approximately 75% to 80% occupancy.
Using an ideal 80% occupancy rate, an estimated nearly 500 of the new 624 rooms in final planning
(soon to be constructed) will be occupied throughout the year. The number of visitors per room
can vary greatly based on business or leisure travel and the class of hotel. If anywhere between 1
and 4 guests stay per room is assumed, an estimated between 500 and 2,000 overnight guests
will stay in Inglewood in these hotels in the future.

The new guests and residents will likely bring additional spending power to the City, presuming
the City can provide these guests with experiential and essential retail offerings that support the
entertainment attractions within the City. It is important to note that the influx of new guests and
residents can put a strain on existing infrastructure and contribute to additional traffic congestion
and emissions. The planned Inglewood Transit Connector project connecting the Hollywood
Park/sports-entertainment complex with the Downtown Inglewood K Line station in the northern
part of the City, can aid in reducing congestion and emissions.

5.1 Land Use
The following sections describe Inglewood’s existing land uses, current General Plan and Zoning
Ordinance land use designations, pending or approved development projects, and sites identified
to meet the County’s Regional Housing Needs Allocation by the City’s adopted Housing Element.
It also includes an overview of the City’s land use planning context, including Specific Plans and
other relevant planning documents, and a description of the City’s significant places and urban
form characteristics and implications. This information establishes a baseline of on-the-ground
uses and existing policies to which potential changes in the land use plan can be compared.

5.1.1 Existing Land Use
As depicted in Table 5-1 and Figure 5-1, Existing Land Use, the City of Inglewood is a largely
residential community consisting primarily of multi-family and single-family residences, which are
intermixed in many areas of the city. Commercial uses are concentrated in the downtown and
along several major streets, including Centinela Avenue, La Brea Avenue, Market Street,
Manchester Boulevard, Century Boulevard, and Prairie Avenue. Though they occupy a smaller
proportion of the city’s land area, commercial uses are growing, and several key projects, including
SoFi Stadium, the Intuit Dome, and Hollywood Park Casino are drawing regional visitors.
Inglewood’s largest open space and recreational use areas, which include a cemetery and public
park, are in the northern part of the city, and industrial uses are concentrated in the west, along
Florence Avenue and adjacent to Interstate 405 (I-405).

Residential

Inglewood’s largest existing land use is residential, comprising approximately 60% of the total
land area. Of this, 1,558 acres (34%) are developed with single-family residences and 1,142 acres
(25%) are single family residences. Mixed residential and commercial residences encompass
26 acres (0.6%), and five acres (0.1%) are developed with mobile homes and trailer park residences.

Single-family residence in Inglewood

Much of the City is developed with neighborhoods containing a mix of single- and multi-family
housing units, largely developed in the early and mid-20th century, particularly in the Arbor Village
and Lockhaven neighborhoods. See Figure 5-2, Neighborhood Map, for the locations of the city’s
neighborhoods. La Tijera Village, Morningside Park, Century Heights, Fairview Heights, and parts
of the Sports Village mostly consist of single-family homes. Neighborhoods developed almost
exclusively with single-family detached housing are generally limited to the eastern side of the
city (east of Inglewood Park Cemetery and the Hollywood Park Entertainment and Sports complex)
and a small pocket in the northwest adjoining the unincorporated View Park-Windsor Hills
neighborhood. Multi-family housing is scattered throughout the community, but significant
clusters are northeast of the Hollywood Park project, north of Florence Avenue, along Crenshaw
Boulevard, and along streets extending north from 104th Street behind Village Shopping Center.

Mixed residential and commercial uses, which are mostly distributed horizontally with commercial
use at the front of the property and residential use at the back, are scattered throughout the city
but concentrated in the western portion of the city, particularly along W. Arbor Vitae Street and
W. Manchester Boulevard. Mobile homes and trailer parks are largely south of Century Boulevard.

Commercial and Services
Commercial and services uses, including individual retail stores, multitenant shopping centers, and
big-box retailers, occupy 677 acres, or approximately 15% of the land in Inglewood—the third
largest land use in the City.

Commercial uses are largely located along the city’s primary transportation corridors, including
portions of Manchester Boulevard, La Brea Avenue, Century Boulevard, Crenshaw Boulevard,
Imperial Highway, Arbor Vitae Street, and Prairie Avenue. Typically, these are developed with
community and neighborhood-serving uses in mostly low-rise buildings on shallow-depth
properties with small-scale single use and multi-tenant shopping centers at key intersections
along their length. Inglewood’s historic downtown area along and adjoining Market Street
contains a mix of retail, restaurant, and similar buildings along well-landscaped and pedestrian-
oriented frontages serving local residents. Larger multi-tenant commercial centers are located
along Century Boulevard between Prairie Avenue and Crenshaw Boulevard (The Village at
Century),the intersection of Crenshaw Boulevard and Imperial Highway (Crenshaw/Imperial
Shopping Center), and at Hollywood Park (The Marketplace).

The most significant concentration of commercially oriented and mixed-use development is the
expanding Entertainment and Sports District northeast of the intersection of Prairie Avenue and
Century Boulevard. Much of the area’s development is anchored by major destination uses such
as SoFi Stadium, Kia Forum, and Intuit Dome, with supporting office, retail, entertainment, and
residential uses. SoFi Stadium hosts the Los Angeles Rams and Los Angeles Chargers of the
National Football League as well as other large-scale sporting events and concerts. Kia Forum
hosts large concerts and other performances. Intuit Dome hosts the Los Angeles Clippers of the
National Basketball League as well as concerts and other performances.

General Office
Office uses comprise 61 acres in the community, accounting for about 1% of its land area. These
are located throughout the city, with concentrations along Centinela Avenue, North Prairie Avenue
adjacent to Inglewood Park Cemetery, and along North La Brea Avenue near Inglewood City Hall.

Some large footprint, multi-tenant professional offices are found along major streets like
La Cienega Boulevard, Prairie Avenue, and La Brea Avenue. Most office uses, however, are
characterized by small, individual tenant buildings.

Industrial
Approximately 5% of the area (213 acres) is developed with industrial uses. These are clustered in
the city’s western area, with a concentration that is bounded by Florence Avenue to the north, I-
405 to the east, West Arbor Vitae Street to the south, and Portal Avenue to the west. Lighter
industrial uses such as trucking, freight, and mailing services are found in the area. Many buildings
are multi-tenant and host a variety of entities. There is minimal warehousing in the area.

Additional industrial land uses are located north of Florence Avenue, south of Hyde Park Boulevard
and North Oak Street, and between I-405 and West Ivy Avenue.

Transportation, Communications, and Utilities
Transportation, communications, and utilities land uses generally consist of infrastructure and
easements supporting the various functions of these systems. These comprise 25 acres, or
approximately 0.5% of land in Inglewood.

Included in this category are properties and facilities owned by the Los Angeles County
Metropolitan Transportation Authority (namely the Metro K Line fixed rail infrastructure),
Inglewood Unified School District (a maintenance facility), and Southern California Edison (an
electrical substation).

Public and Quasi-Public Facilities
Inglewood’s public and quasi-public facilities are operated by federal, state, and local-level (city
and county of Los Angeles) entities. This land use category includes police, sheriff, and fire stations;
  major healthcare and medical centers (e.g., Centinela
  Hospital Medical Center); some educational institutions
  (St. Mary’s Academy); post offices; religious institutions;
  and more. Properties developed for these uses occupy
  187 acres, or approximately 4% of the total land area.

  Open Space and Recreation
  Open space and recreation land uses generally consist of
  local parks and other reserved open spaces and
  recreation areas. These uses occupy 390 acres,
  representing approximately 9% of Inglewood’s land—the
  fourth-largest land use in the city.

  Open space and recreation acreage consists of
  Inglewood Park Cemetery, which was founded in 1905
  and occupies 200 acres. Directly north, on the opposite
  side of East Florence Avenue from the cemetery, is
  Edward Vincent Jr. Park, the city’s largest municipal park
  at 55 acres.
 St. John Chrysostom Church in Inglewood

The remainder of the open space and recreation land use areas include smaller parks such as
Ashwood Park, Center Park, Centinela Adobe Park, Circle Park, Grevillea Park, Queen Park, Siminski
Park, North Park, Rogers Park, and Darby Park.

Education

Education uses occupy 206 acres or approximately 5% of the City’s land area, and consist of both
public and private grade and technical schools and institutions of higher education that are
located across the city. These include but are not limited to Bennett/Kew Academy, Morningside
High School, Inglewood High School, Crozier Middle School, Centinela Elementary School, Frank
D. Parent Elementary School, and University of West Los Angeles.

Under Construction

Approximately 22 acres of Inglewood’s land was under construction at the time this data was
published in 2019, representing about 0.5% of the total land area. These projects included SoFi
Stadium. The acreage and types of uses in this category will change over time as construction is
completed and new projects undertaken.

Building under construction at intersection of La Brea Avenue and Regent Street in Inglewood

Vacant

Approximately 75 acres of Inglewood’s land is vacant, representing close to 2% of the total land
area. This acreage primarily consists of small, scattered parcels and greenbelts and rights-of-way
within residential project areas.

Some larger parcels, though identified as vacant in the most recent data, have since been
developed. This is the case at the intersections of North Inglewood Avenue and Beach Avenue
and North Eucalyptus Avenue and Beach Avenue.

5.1.2 Current General Plan Land Use
The General Plan Land Use Diagram (Figure 5-3), published in 2023, represents the City’s policy
for the distribution and intensity of use that is permitted for development. Table 5-2 describes the
types of use, their total acreage, and their percentage of Inglewood’s overall land area. It should
be noted that the diagram in Figure 5-3 is generalized, and boundaries of land use designations
do not correspond precisely to parcels lines, streets, or other geographic references. This
generality makes it difficult for the City to comply with legislation requiring consistency of zoning
with the General Plan and recent housing legislation (AB 821, 2023) establishing the Land Use
Plan’s designations as the default for determining housing development approvals. In addition,
the diagram may not accurately reflect as-built conditions.

General Plan Land Use Designations, Intensities, and Descriptions

The Land Use Element of Inglewood’s General Plan was comprehensively updated in 1980 and
most recently amended in 2016. Some of the current land use designations on the City’s General
Plan Land Use Diagram are not included in the Land Use Element.

Residential

The element calls for a pattern of regulation which allows flexibility for the future yet maintains a
framework that is consistent with good land use and the retention of single-family neighborhoods.
It notes that higher intensity uses should be located around the civic center and along major
arterials, thus facilitating mass transit and preventing the large traffic volumes associated with
multi-family housing from passing through and disrupting less intensely developed residential
areas.

•  Low Density. The density standards for this class, which is largely single-family
  neighborhoods, provide for from one to six units to the acre. The element designates that
  these neighborhoods be preserved and maintained.

•  Low-Medium Density. These areas are presently developed primarily as single-family
  residences and are intended to be well located with respect to convenience and access to the
  regional transportation network and serve as buffers or transition areas between more
  intensive development and areas of less intensive use. This category has a relatively flexible
  density standard of from seven to twenty-two dwelling units to the acre.

•  Medium Density. Medium density residential development is generally proposed for those
  areas surrounding the downtown business district and Civic Center, which provides ideal
  access to the regional freeway network and close-in convenience to the major shopping
  facilities of the downtown business district. The density range for this designation is twenty-
  three to forty-three dwelling units per acre.

Commercial Land Use

There are three categories of commercial usage in the Land Use Element: commercial, which
represents all forms of commercial enterprise; commercial/residential, which represents areas
where planning and development standards can be used to allow mixed commercial and
residential use; and commercial/recreational, which is the area where both commercial and private
recreation and similar uses would be allowed.

Building intensity standards for commercial uses are already controlled by the City's zoning
ordinance, and no additional regulations are proposed by the element.

The Land Use Element describes “regional” commercial facilities as being located in the Central
Business District and Crenshaw-Imperial Shopping Center; "community" facilities providing retail
and services along most major traffic arterials; and "neighborhood" convenience shopping areas
dispersed throughout the city at locations in or adjacent to the neighborhoods served. In addition,
the element proposes areas for "mixed use," especially commercial-residential and commercial-

recreational. Such areas of mixed use are intended to promote the most efficient use of the city's
land resources.

Major Mixed Use

The Major Mixed Use land use designation was added to the Land Use Element effective July 8,
2009. The category encompasses approximately 238 acres of land at the site of the former
Hollywood Park racetrack that has been and continues to be developed with various commercial,
open space, civic, recreation, and residential uses. The combination of residential and non-
residential land uses is permitted consistent with the Hollywood Park Specific Plan. Residential
development is not to exceed 85 dwelling units per acre, except as specified in the California
Government Code Section 65915-65918 or as established in the City’s Municipal Code or an
adopted plan amendment. The height limitation in the Major Mixed Use category is 75 feet for
residential structures and 150 feet for commercial uses, excluding architectural or sign elements.

Industrial Land Use
The element designates only one category of industrial use, which encompasses both light and
heavy industrial. Generally, Inglewood’s industrial areas feature light manufacturing, assembly,
and wholesale/warehousing facilities and activities.

Public/Semi-public Land Use
The Land Use Element describes Public/Semi-public Land Use as areas including city hall, library,
police station, parking structure, health centers and hospitals, county building, fire station, and
schools. The General Plan Land Use Map does not reflect this, however, as several of those areas
are considered part of the Downtown Transit Oriented Development category or another
designation.

Open Space Land Use

This designation distinguishes lands and uses that should be reserved for open space and/or
recreational activities.

Hospital-Medical/Residential Land Use
As stated in the Land Use Element, this classification was an outgrowth of a specialized land use
situation. At the time, Inglewood had two regional medical centers that were a dominating
influence on the land pattern in the area in which they were located. One has since closed. The
areas designated on the map include related uses in proximity to those centers, which might
include offices, pharmacies, and nursing homes. In these areas, hospital-related uses and
residential uses are permitted.

Downtown Transit Oriented District
The Downtown Transit Oriented District consists principally of the half-mile radius around the
Downtown Inglewood Metro Station and is divided into seven subdistricts: Historic Downtown,
Civic Center, TechTown, Beach Avenue, Fairview West, Hillcrest, and Queen Street. It is intended

light industrial/creative office in a pedestrian-friendly environment that facilitates transit usage.

Fairview Heights Transit Oriented District

The Fairview Heights Transit Oriented District consists principally of the Inglewood side of the
half-mile radius around the Fairview Heights Metro Station. Much of the TOD is the historic, low-
density residential neighborhood of Fairview Heights. The station-adjacent area that fronts West
Boulevard, Redondo Boulevard, and Florence Avenue is intended to be a gateway to the city for
transit riders and drivers entering from the east and provide an appropriate connection to Vincent
Park. The Fairview Heights TOD land use category allows for institutional, residential, and/or retail
uses.

General Plan Land Uses Not Described in Land Use Element

Inglewood’s General Plan land use diagram was most recently updated in September 2023 and
now includes four categories that are not described in the land use element.

Inglewood Basketball Entertainment Center corresponds to the recently constructed Intuit Dome.
Descriptions of the Crenshaw/Imperial TOD and Westchester/Veterans TOD categories can be
found in Section 5.4, Approved Specific Plans.

5.1.3 Existing Zoning
The City of Inglewood’s zoning categories are defined in Chapter 12 of the Inglewood Municipal
Code and depicted on the City’s Zoning Map (Figure 5-4). The zoning categories are the City’s

regulating the physical form of structures on each parcel (e.g., density/intensity, building height
and setbacks, parking requirements, and so on). The zoning districts provide specificity and
greater detail regarding the categories of use delineated by the General Plan, while maintaining
consistency with its uses and densities.

Overlay Zones

In addition to a Sign Overlay Zone located in and around the Hollywood Park development,
Inglewood’s Municipal Code includes six other overlay zones with specific objectives, regulations
and standards related to land use and overall character.

Art Deco Overlay Zone
The Art Deco Overlay Zone is guided by Art Deco Design standards in the City’s municipal code,
which address architectural features, lighting, landscaping, signage, and more. The overlay applies
to General Commercial zoned properties in the northeast portion of the city along Manchester
Boulevard.

Classic/Vintage Car Sales Overlay Zone

This overlay zone is associated with uses where fine or distinctive automobiles over twenty-five
years of age are sold or displayed. The Classic/Vintage Car Sales Overlay Zone is located along
portions of Centinela and North La Brea Avenues in the northwest part of Inglewood.

January 2025 | CITY OF INGLEWOOD | EXISTING CONDITIONS REPORT  Page 5-15

Live-Work Overlay Zone

As stated in the City’s Code of Ordinances, the objectives of the live-work overlay zone and live-
work regulations are to 1) allow accessory residential uses in existing nonresidential structures, in
areas of the City that are appropriate locations for live-work uses, 2) allow live-work units that
function primarily as workspaces that also contain ancillary residential space in each unit, 3) allow
for the architecturally appropriate incorporation of residential uses into existing nonresidential
structures, to ensure that any modifications seamlessly enhance the structures and are compatible
with the surrounding commercial or industrial area's design character, and to maintain the
physical characteristics that are typical for areas of commerce (e.g., business signage, commercial
street frontage), and 4) protect existing or potential commercial and industrial uses from
displacement and/or conflicts that can arise from the introduction of residential uses.

Applicable to the conversion of existing structures in a commercial or manufacturing zone within
the overlay, the zone’s design standards address unit size, floor area, height, and more. The overlay
applies in several areas of the city, including Downtown Inglewood and the Fairview Heights and
La Tijera Village neighborhoods.

Medical Enterprise Overlay Zone

The Medical Enterprise Overlay is applicable to the Residential and Medical (R-M) and General
Commercial (C-2) zoned properties adjacent to Inglewood Park Cemetery and in the areas
surrounding Centinela Hospital Medical Center.

Mixed-Use Overlay Zone (Morningside Park)
The objective of the Mixed-Use Overlay Zone in the Morningside Park neighborhood is to provide
for residential/retail mixed-use development opportunities suitable for the center of the South
Inglewood Gateway District. Permitted uses are identified in the Crenshaw Imperial Transit
Oriented Development Plan as well as accessory dwelling units, and restaurants.

Transportation Corridor Overlay Zone
The Transportation Corridor Overlay Zone was put in place to ensure orderly development of
expanded transportation facilities, specifically the Metro K Line, and the nearby employment,
housing, and activity hubs. The area is unique as the transit project spans multiple underlying
zones and requires integration with public rights-of-way. The overlay generally follows the path
of the future Inglewood Transit Connector connecting the Downtown Inglewood Metro station to
major sports and entertainment destinations: Kia Forum, SoFi Stadium, Hollywood Park Casino,
and the Intuit Dome.

5.1.4 Approved Specific Plans
Inglewood International Business Park Specific Plan

Prepared in 1993, the Inglewood International Business Park Specific Plan establishes land use,
infrastructure requirements, and the design character for the 44-acre area bounded by 102nd
Street to the north, Yukon Avenue to the east, 104th street to the south, and Prairie Avenue to the
west. The area, which was designated “Industrial” in the City’s Land Use Element at the time, was
envisioned as an aesthetically pleasing business park to facilitate large-scale corporate users while
benefitting the City and the residents who live in the surrounding neighborhood.

The plan’s land use development standards provide for the continued existence and new
development of compatible uses that facilitate large-scale corporate users and generate
employment and revenue base for the City, outlining two zoning designations: General
Commercial (C-2) and Limited Manufacturing (M-1L). A small parcel concept, large parcel concept,
and proposed circulation system are included in the plan as well.

The urban development standards address siting, massing, height, and architectural character to
provide a framework and create visual unity. The plan also discusses visitor parking areas, parking
structures, building design and architecture signage, site furniture, sidewalks, and landscaping.
Circulation, site access, and parking development standards provide an on-site circulation system
and introduce measures to minimally impact surrounding roadways.

In addition to land use development standards, the plan includes urban design development,
circulation, public works and services, and environment development standards.

Village Specific Plan

Prepared in December 1998, the Village Specific Plan sought to “return a quality of life and
neighborhood livability” to Inglewood’s Darby-Dixon neighborhood, which is at the southwest
corner of West Century Boulevard and South Crenshaw Boulevard. The plan’s major strategies are
a physical overhaul of public and private spaces, new framework within the neighborhood with
the City commitment to turning the neighborhood around, and a broad ranging yet focused
implementation plan.

To achieve the vision of a neighborhood that is balanced with commercial, residential, educational,
and recreational opportunities, the plan outlines a shift from residential to commercial land uses.
Commercial expansion, improvements to the circulation system, the establishment of park and
recreation spaces, and the creation of neighborhood identity through landscape changes were
considered effective ways of revitalizing the neighborhood.

The specific plan includes primary and supporting concept plans, implementation strategies, and
development regulations and guidelines, which address commercial building design and layout,
residential uses, landscaping, signage, lighting, and more.

Hollywood Park Specific Plan

The Hollywood Park Specific Plan provides a land use framework for the redevelopment of the
238-acre Hollywood Park site, creating a pedestrian oriented regional retail destination with a mix
of parks, retail, housing, entertainment, and more. The plan addresses development location and
intensity, land use categories, and building heights. Preparation of the specific plan included
community involvement and resulted in development standards, design guidelines, proposed
infrastructure improvements, and methods for implementation and administration. First adopted
in July 2009, the plan was amended in September 2014 and February 2015.

Hollywood Park Specific Plan cover page

The Specific Plan’s sixth chapter, “Stadium Alternative Project Standards,” was written to be
applied if a development applicant elected to build a stadium at Hollywood Park. The chapter was
adopted through a voter initiative process, and the applicant ultimately elected to build the
stadium (now known as SoFi Stadium), making Chapter 6 the applicable zoning standards for land
uses in the Hollywood Park Specific Plan area.

Chapter 6 identified the land uses within the Hollywood Park Specific Plan area:

  •  Open Space  •  Civic
  •  Mixed-Use  •  Sports and Entertainment
  •  Residential  •  Interim Land Uses
  •  Commercial and Recreation

5.1.6 Airport Impacts
Several plans focusing on airport land use, particularly at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX),
have implications for the City of Inglewood.

Published in 1991 and revised in 2004, the Los Angeles County Airport Land Use Commission’s
Comprehensive Land Use Plan establishes planning boundaries for the eleven general aviation
airports in the region. Inglewood’s southernmost boundary is separated from Hawthorne
Municipal Airport’s boundary by only I-105 and 120th Street, leaving less than 1,000 feet of
separation. LAX’s planning boundary crosses the City of Inglewood’s, overlapping parts of the City
with a variety of land uses, including industrial, commercial, and residential. The planning
boundaries for both airports are shown in Figure 5-13.

Areas determined by the Airport Land Use Commission are subject to safety hazards, which
warrant certain height restrictions and the establishment of approach surface and runway
protection zones. Maximum building heights are specified by the Federal Aviation Administration
regulations and restrictions, which generally limit building heights to 200 feet within 20,000 feet
of an airport. Noise, which can have physiological, psychological, sociological, and economic
effects, is also a significant factor within these planning boundaries.

The LAX Specific Plan divides into four land use subareas the area bounded by 88th Street,
Manchester Avenue, and 91st Street on the north; Imperial Highway on the south; Pershing Drive
on the west, and La Cienega Boulevard on the east. While none falls within the City of Inglewood’s
boundary, the Airport Landside and Airport Landside Support subareas are immediately adjacent
to Inglewood along the city’s western border, which follows La Cienega Boulevard to the west and
Arbor Vitae Street to the north. These are primarily industrial and commercial areas of the city,
with some scattered education facilities and multi-family residential uses. The purpose of the
Airport Landside and Airport Landside Support subareas are to allow for the safe and efficient
operation of airport facilities, primarily providing access to the airport and processing passengers.
Uses in the Commercial (C2) and Light Industrial (M2) zoning categories in the LA Municipal Code
are permitted. Aircraft under power and buildings containing dwelling units are prohibited.

The LAX Specific Plan has been in effect since 2005. As part of the General Plan of the City of Los
Angeles, the LAX Plan was prepared in 2017. Its goals are to:

•  Strengthen LAX’s unique role within the regional airport network as the international gateway
  to the Southern California region.

•  Develop and maintain the highest standards of air traffic safety and passenger security
  through design and the latest innovations.

•  Optimize LAX’s critical role in supporting the economy as a major generator of economic
  activity.

•  Recognize the responsibility to minimize effects on the physical environment.

•  Acknowledge neighborhood context and promote compatibility between LAX and the
  surrounding neighborhoods.

•  Improve ground access to LAX.

The LAX Plan and LAX Specific Plan are not independent documents, using the same categories
of subareas. The LAX Plan specifies that the aspects of passenger and cargo movement in the
Inglewood-adjacent Airport Landside area are the Central Terminal Area, Intermodal
Transportation Facilities, the Consolidated Rental Car Facility, and the Automated People Mover
system. The LAX Plan establishes a land use policy framework, and the LAX Specific Plan
establishes zoning and development regulations and standards. The specific plan is a tool for
achieving the goals and implementing the policies and programs of the LAX Plan and establishes
the procedures for processing future specific projects and activities anticipated under the LAX
Master Plan Program.

Downtown Inglewood

Downtown Inglewood straddles three major thoroughfares—La Brea Avenue, Manchester
Boulevard, and Florence Avenue. This area of the city encompasses the civic core and includes
Inglewood City Hall, Inglewood Public Library, and other city and county facilities and buildings.

Building along Market Street in Inglewood

Market Street, a pedestrian-oriented commercial district established in 1908 and rehabilitated
during the 1990s, was historically the site of community gathering and center of commercial
activity for the city’s Black residents. Its revitalization is a priority for the community, and steps
toward that objective have been taken and are underway or planned, including streetscaping and
placemaking improvements and mixed-use development projects.

Sports and Entertainment District/Hollywood Park Mixed-Use Development

SoFi Stadium, Kia Forum and Hollywood Park Casino anchor Inglewood’s Hollywood Park sports
and entertainment district, which was formerly home to the Hollywood Park Racetrack. This 300-
acre master-planned development houses office space, condominiums, a movie theater, outdoor
spaces, a hotel, YouTube Theater, restaurants, and other commercial uses. The objective for
development in this district is to create a vibrant regional destination for tenants, residents, and
visitors, harmonizing a variety of land uses. Hollywood Park construction began in 2014, and its
retail district, which is fully built out to the maximum area of 890,000 square feet, opened in Fall

Metro K Line Station Areas

Several Metro K Line stations are within the Inglewood’s boundaries: Fairview Heights Station,
Downtown Inglewood Station, and Westchester/Veterans Station.

Westchester/Veterans is off Florence Avenue along the city’s western boundary. Its surrounding
land uses are primarily industrial and commercial. Of the three Metro K Line stations in the city,
Westchester/Veterans is less integrated with its immediate surroundings. However, it is proximate
to local restaurants like Randy’s Donuts and the historic Centinela Adobe. It provides transit
connections to the Metro C and K Line Link, which provides free bus service between the
Westchester/Veterans and Aviation/LAX Station (C Line) running on the same schedule as trains.

Downtown Inglewood Station is proximate to entertainment destinations such as the Miracle
Theater. Station amenities include bike lockers and bike racks. From the Downtown Inglewood
Station, transit riders can connect to Metro 40, 111, 211, 212, and 215 and Torrance Transit 10.
Land uses surrounding the station are a mix of Commercial, Industrial, and Multi- and Single-
Family Residential, and it is near pedestrian-oriented areas like Market Street.

Inglewood Park Cemetery

Founded in 1905, Inglewood Park Cemetery is the city’s largest land use area in the Open Space
and Recreation category. The cemetery’s 200 acres make it a uniquely large green space in the
city. The cemetery is open to the public from sunrise to sunset. While recreation such as jogging

services, or graves.

Residential and Mixed-Use Neighborhoods

Many of Inglewood’s residential neighborhoods, including La Tijera Village, Fairview Heights, and
Morningside Park, consist primarily of single-family detached homes on small lots with scattered
apartment and multi-family buildings.

Mixed-use neighborhoods are small in comparison and located on the edges of neighborhoods
like Centinela Heights, Arbor Village, Morningside Park, Lockhaven, and Sports Village close to
commercial corridors along major streets such as Centinela Avenue, Manchester Boulevard, South
Prairie Avenue, and W. Imperial Highway.

5.1.8 Land Use/Urban Form Implications for Greenhouse Gas Emissions
  and Climate Change
In California in 2021, approximately 39 percent of greenhouse gas emissions, the primary
contributor to climate change, were attributable to transportation sources. 1 Vehicle trips
generated and miles traveled are directly related the distribution and densities of land use.
In Inglewood, uses are segregated and low to medium density—single family neighborhoods,
multifamily apartment communities, and multitenant commercial centers. Consequently, most
trips away from home for jobs, shopping, entertainment, and recreation are by car. Most
commercial centers have uses that serve as single-point destinations—a grocery store for
example—unlike newer, pedestrian-active “experiential” centers where people walk among and
patronize multiple stores, dine, and enjoy music and the presence of their friends in an
environment designed with pleasant outdoor spaces and amenities. Travel to and from multiple
single-point destinations worsens air quality and increases greenhouse gas emissions,
exacerbating the effects of climate change.
As new development in Inglewood proceeds as infill or replaces underutilized and economically
obsolete uses, there will be opportunities to create a greater mix and intensity of land uses that
reduce vehicle trips and make areas attractive for walking, bicycling, and other forms of personal
and public transit. Land use patterns that lessen the need for the automobile can have a significant
benefit by reducing Inglewood’s greenhouse gas emissions and climate change impacts. Recent
and proposed transit improvements such as the K Line extension, Inglewood Transit Connector,
and the implementation of various TOD Plans can have a beneficial impact in reducing vehicle
miles traveled as well.

5.1.9 Housing Element Sites
The City’s 6th Cycle Housing Element covers the 2021-2029 planning period and contains the
City’s plan and policies to provide opportunities for (and not unduly constrain) housing
development sufficient to meet the housing needs of everyone in the community. As a part of this
plan, the Housing Element includes an inventory of sites suitable for the development of housing
that will accommodate projections described in the Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA).
The identification of the housing element sites utilizes the zoning regulations in place at the time
of adoption, thus rezoning to meet RHNA is unnecessary.
The City of Inglewood’s required 7,439 RHNA units are split across four income levels—very low,
low, moderate, and above moderate. The extremely low income need can be calculated as 50% of
the very-low income RHNA, or 906 units.

5.1.10  Findings
Community Insights Regarding Land Use

Common concerns and desires related to land use emerged in conversations with community
members during the public outreach activities described in Chapter 1. Many people expressed
feeling positive about new development in the city while some asked that local government
officials engage residents proactively about future land use changes. In addition, there is a desire
for better compatibility between local existing businesses and residences with regional
entertainment activity. Commenters were effusive in appreciation for their neighborhoods, the
City’s parks, the responsiveness of City staff, and the sense of community.

For many, a priority is the restoration and reinvigoration of Market Street and Downtown
Inglewood with greater commercial activity at an appropriate scale. Several corridors were
similarly identified by community members as being optimal for mixed-use development,
including Imperial Boulevard, Century Boulevard, and Prairie Avenue. A greater mix of land uses
is sought in multiple areas of the city. Objections to “high rises” were also raised by some.

Some community members shared that existing land use regulations, zoning designations, and
permitting processes have sometimes created obstacles in the case of opening businesses,
establishing urban agriculture sites, and more. Concerns were also raised with visual blight, with
some expressing an interest in improving vacant buildings and empty lots and the appearance of
warehouses along Century Boulevard.

A desire for additional housing choices was also noted in several comments. Specific housing
types mentioned include low-income housing and affordable homes, housing for seniors and
veterans, accessory dwelling units (ADU) and workforce housing. Stakeholders are also interested
in more single-family housing, preserving existing housing and being attentive to the impacts of
ADUs, particularly on parking supply.

The inclusion of more public park space and enhancement of existing public park space were
popular requests. Improving streetscapes was also a priority. Finally, community members posed
questions about how land use designations might change for Inglewood Unified School District
school sites that face future closure.

Planning Implications

As a highly urbanized and built-out area, the City of Inglewood has few parcels remaining for
development. Future development will need to be infill or replace existing uses. A number of
major infill projects are underway and have set a precedent for this type of development in the
city, including Hollywood Park. The City’s TOD Plans guide infill development in strategic areas to
maximize access to the region’s expanding transit network. However, changes to additional land
use designations and/or policies may be warranted to support integration with the planned
Inglewood Transit Connector.

The long term viability of Inglewood’s linear commercial corridors is tenuous. They consist of a
mix of uses but face a number of challenges, such as lack of parking and retail turnover and

uncertainty about maintenance, improvement, and appropriate uses over time. These corridors
have the potential to serve as centers of neighborhood activity in the way that the Market Street
District has in the past and aims to do again.

In terms of climate impacts, the City’s current development pattern and reliance on automobiles
as the primary means of transportation affect air quality and levels of greenhouse gas emissions,
public health, and residents’ quality of life. However, recent investments in transportation
infrastructure—the construction of K Line transit stations and the planned Inglewood Transit
Connector—and the integration of future development with this infrastructure provides
opportunities to lessen negative climate impacts.

Inglewood’s General Plan Land Use Diagram is challenging to utilize due to its generality and its
incompatibility with geographic references. Its current format makes it difficult for the City to
maintain consistency with the Zoning Map and comply with state legislation. For those reasons,
an entirely new General Plan Land Use Diagram will be prepared through this General Plan Update
effort. In addition, it is unclear if the land use designations described in the Land Use Element and
utilized in the Land Use Diagram are appropriate to address the land use types found in the City
today and desired in the future.

5.2 Urban Form
The following sections describe Inglewood’s urban form. The City’s physical form and design
character speak to how people experience the community and their perceptions of the quality of
life. Urban form plays a critical role in the creation of distinctive places and the establishment of
a unique identity for the community and its neighborhoods. Urban form not only relates to
aesthetic character but also impacts community vitality, stability and function. There are both
beneficial and detrimental implications related to form for fundamental issues such as business
activity, traffic congestion, transit use, air pollution, and climate change.

Much of the city is organized around an orthogonal street grid, meaning streets intersect at right
angles. Areas in Inglewood with greater topographic diversity, however, have more discontinuous
and curvilinear streets, particularly in the northern part of the city. Inglewood’s continuous grid
has gaps in several locations, including the Sports and Entertainment District, planned residential
developments, large format commercial centers, and educational and medical campuses. The
pattern also differs in Downtown Inglewood where a portion of the street grid is oriented at a 45
degree angle from surrounding, cardinally oriented streets.

Two major interstates, I-405 and I-105, partially form the City’s western and southern boundaries.
The northern and eastern edges divide Inglewood from the City of Los Angeles. However, the
distinction between the two cities is subtle because the urban form along and surrounding the
boundary lines have very similar residential typologies.

Inglewood’s developed pattern is dominated by traditional and multi-family residential
neighborhoods; commercial centers and corridors concentrated along arterial roads; industrial
areas; a large sports and entertainment district; and dispersed open spaces and office, education,
and medical campuses. Aside from undeveloped portions of Hollywood Park in the Sports and

occupied by Edward J. Vincent Park and Inglewood Park Cemetery, Inglewood is mostly built out.

5.2.1 Natural Elements
Topography and Vistas

Inglewood’s topography has influenced the city’s built environment and natural scenery. Certain
areas have more pronounced elevation changes than others. Northern portions of the city,
particularly around Centinela Heights, La Tijera Village, and Fairview Heights, have more varied
terrain, with gently rolling hills that provide scenic views of the Los Angeles Basin. To the west and
north, respectively, one can see the Pacific Ocean and skyline of downtown Los Angeles from the
city’s highest points. Areas in the western and southern parts of the city, closer to Los Angeles
International Airport, are relatively flat, creating a more uniform topography in both commercial
and residential areas.

Hydrology and Watershed

The City’s hydrology is shaped by its position in the larger Ballona Creek watershed, which drains
much of the surrounding urban area into the Pacific Ocean. The flatter western and southern
portions of Inglewood contribute to surface water runoff that flows to Ballona Creek. Areas with
more varied terrain create localized drainage patterns, which feed into smaller tributaries.

The City’s stormwater systems direct water from streets and neighborhoods into concrete
channels that connect to Ballona Creek and other regional waterways. Downstream from the Los
Angeles River, Inglewood’s regional water flow patterns are impacted during heavy rain events.

Open Space and Trails

Inglewood’s largest parks—Edward Vincent Jr. Park, Rogers Park, and Darby Park—provide a
range of facilities and recreational opportunities, such as sports fields, picnic areas, an aquatic
center, tennis courts, and more. Uniquely, Inglewood Park Cemetery, with its parklike grounds,
provides a place where visitors can enjoy walking paths. In addition, the Inglewood Civic Center
and Hollywood Park development have incorporated open spaces.

There is no direct access in the city to regional trail networks such as the Park to Playa Trail, which
connects the Baldwin Hills parklands to the Pacific Ocean. However, Inglewood is close to key
trailheads in neighboring communities such as the Ballona Creek Bike Path. There is also an
extensive trail network in nearby Kenneth Hahn State Recreation Area.

Each of these three categories are further distilled into subcategories. The typical characteristics
for each of these elements are explained below.

Block and Parcel Size

•  Block Size. Block size is one of the most important defining characteristics of a community.
  Typically, smaller blocks support more pedestrian activity.

•  Block Footprint. Closely related to block size, the proportions of a block affect the character
  of a community. The length and width ratio of a block plays an important role in building types
  and the location of other elements such as parking. It may also affect pedestrian access,
  particularly across wide boulevards with few crosswalks.

•  Parcel Size. Parcel size is an indicator of scale within a neighborhood or district. Large parcels
  are typically found in automobile-oriented environments. Smaller parcels typically result in a
  finer-grained development pattern that is more conducive to walking.

Streets and Intersections

•  Travel Lanes. Roadways with multiple travel lanes accommodate higher traffic volumes and
  can act as barriers between the land uses on either side. Conversely, narrower streets with
  fewer travel lanes can create more comfortable environments that encourage pedestrian
  activities. The width of travel lanes also contributes to perceptions of safety and walkability.

•  Intersections. Intersections are a good indicator of a neighborhood’s internal level of
  accessibility and are related to block size. Typically, a higher number of intersections ensures
  many possible routes of travel by foot, bike, or automobile. Conversely, fewer intersections
  can indicate greater dependence on arterial and collector streets to accommodate automobile
  traffic.

•  Parking Location. The location and distribution of off-street parking are indicated in the front,
  to the side, and/or to the rear of buildings. Parking may also be in an under- or above-ground
  parking structure.

Building and Site Features

•  Activity Based Model. Buildings are mapped to show the relationship between built and
  unbuilt space. This shows spatially the size, arrangement, and configuration of buildings
  throughout the city.

•  Building Location and Frontage. Frontage and building location describe the relationship of
  buildings to streets and distinguishes the various types of street character of an area. Building
  frontage may be a proxy for the quality of pedestrian experience, because buildings with
  greater connectivity to the street and sidewalk are more welcoming to those on foot.

5.2.3 Findings
Inglewood’s physical form and design give texture and identity to the city’s neighborhoods and
community places. The urban form is defined by man-made elements, including blocks and
parcels, streets, and building footprints and location.

Inglewood’s structure and density primarily support travel and access by automobile. While
single-family housing and multifamily apartments are mixed, neighborhoods are separated from
places of business and employment. Retail and office uses are designed for the automobile, with
limited pedestrian amenities and access. These forms of development contribute negatively to
elements of residents’ quality of life, such as air quality, climate change, and human health. An
exception to this is the Market Street district, where vehicular travel lanes number no more than
three, and commercial buildings are directly along a wide sidewalk with streetscape amenities,
contributing to a more active pedestrian environment. With little vacancy in the city, development
of new uses will require replacement, infill, and/or intensification of the existing built environment.

The analysis in this chapter suggests opportunities and/or constraints for enhancing existing
places and creating quality new places. For example, areas dominated by commercial centers with
large surface parking lots and wide setbacks are likely to remain auto oriented unless
redevelopment of surface parking lots occurs or strategies to make them more pedestrian-friendly
can be implemented. Similarly, wide, commercial corridors with vehicular-exclusive travel lanes do
not provide safe or comfortable infrastructure for cyclists and pedestrians. There may be potential
in both residential neighborhoods and commercial corridors to create more mixed-use
opportunities, bringing residents closer to other forms of development that they frequent.

The City of Inglewood’s circulation system facilitates travel by multiple modes including walking,
bicycling, public transit, motor vehicles, freight, and more. It connects travelers to housing,
employment opportunities, world-class sports and entertainment venues, and local and regional
destinations throughout the city and the greater Los Angeles area. This extensive transportation
network serves the daily mobility needs of all types of users, including residents, visitors,
employers, and more. The existing conditions of these transportation networks, services, and
systems are described in detail in this chapter, along with implications for updating the Circulation
Element in the City’s General Plan.

6.1 Inglewood’s Circulation System
6.1.1 Purposes
Inglewood’s circulation system serves many functions. Its primary purpose is to allow for safe and
efficient travel for people using all modes of transportation to access their destinations. The
mobility system allows residents to reach local-serving retail, schools, residential neighborhoods,
and more, as well as regional destinations in adjacent cities and beyond.

In addition to its transportation functions, the City’s public rights-of-way also play an important
role in placemaking and urban development. In particular, the design of rights-of-way can have
an important role in creating local landmarks and destinations and supporting adjacent land uses.

6.1.2 A Transforming Mobility Network
Just like the city itself, Inglewood’s mobility network is a story of transformation. The existing
circulation system is oriented to vehicles; however, it is evolving and poised for a future that
supports multiple modes of transportation.

In the last few decades, new developments have not only left a lasting imprint on the City’s
physical landscape, but also created new challenges and opportunities for the City’s mobility
network. SOFI Stadium and the Hollywood Park Development Project, redeveloped Kia Forum,
and new Intuit Dome bring in visitors that help boost the City’s economy, but they also lead to
increased traffic volumes and congestion on surrounding streets. Meanwhile, the opening of the
LA Metro K Line has expanded transit access for city residents, opening new options for travel.

In tandem with these changes, the City has prepared several transportation planning-related
documents to support a changing cityscape. In 2022, the City adopted the Active Transportation
and Safe Routes to School Plan, which provides a framework for enhancing pedestrian and bicycle
infrastructure throughout the city. The City also developed plans for Transit Oriented
Development (TOD) around four LA Metro stations along the K and C Lines. Separately, the City
commissioned a Mobility Plan in 2019 that promotes a range of transportation strategies to
address the challenges stemming from new sports and entertainment venues.
