6.2 Transportation Planning Framework
Transportation planning and implementation in the city is governed by many city departments
and regional/state agencies, each with its own functions and responsibilities. In most instances,
the agencies collaborate to develop the plans or policies that apply to the City’s circulation system.
Some plans and policies were adopted/approved by the City of Inglewood, while others were
developed by regional transportation agencies such as the Los Angeles County Metropolitan
Transportation Authority (LA Metro) and the Southern California Association of Governments, and
state and federal agencies. The following offers synopses of the agencies involved as well as
applicable transportation planning efforts and policies.

6.2.1 Agency Involvement
City of Inglewood
The circulation system in Inglewood is primarily planned, implemented, and maintained by the
City of Inglewood. The City owns the majority of the public rights-of-way and is the lead agency
for many transportation projects within its boundaries. The City collaborates with the following
agencies on transportation projects that are outside of the City’s jurisdiction.

Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority
LA Metro plans, operates, and oversees funding for most of the public transportation system in
LA County, including transit and highway projects. The agency is also responsible for planning
and operation of the LA Metro transit system, which has four rail stations in Inglewood as well as
numerous fixed bus routes.

Southern California Association of Governments

The Southern California Association of Governments is the regional transportation planning
agency and metropolitan planning organization for the Southern California region. Among its
many functions, the agency develops the regional long-range transportation plans for the six-
county Southern California region.

California Department of Transportation

Caltrans has authority over the State highway system, including main-line facilities, interchanges,
and arterial state routes. The agency approves the planning and design of improvements for all
State-controlled transportation facilities. Caltrans facilities in or serving Inglewood include I-405
and I-105.

6.2.2 City of Inglewood Plans and Policies
Inglewood Mobility Plan (2019)

In 2019, the City of Inglewood Public Works Department created the City of Inglewood Mobility
Plan. The Plan seeks to create a multimodal city that can sustainably accommodate future
development. The core goals of the Plan include environmental considerations; neighborhood
protections and preservation; an efficient, balanced, and multimodal mobility network; congestion
reduction; and the safety, accessibility, and reliability of the transportation system.

The plan provides goals, policies, and implementation steps for a comprehensive active
transportation network that integrates bicycle and pedestrian enhancements while addressing
ADA requirements. It contains an extensive discussion of existing conditions of existing pedestrian
and bicycle infrastructure in the city, as well as a pedestrian and bicycle collisions analysis. The
plan also provides mini-plans with cut sheets for 17 schools as a part of the Safe Routes to School
component.

6.3 Travel Characteristics
Travel characteristics such as housing-employment dynamics, commute patterns, and commuter
modal split provide insights into how people travel throughout the city.

6.3.1 Housing-Employment Dynamics
Most Inglewood residents travel outside of the city to access employment. According to the 2022
American Community Survey and the 2021 Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics Origin
Destination Employment Statistics, the City has 108,806 residents and 28,070 jobs. Approximately
9.8 percent of total jobs within Inglewood, or 2,757 jobs, are held by Inglewood residents, while
the other 90 percent of jobs are held by those who live elsewhere. The top workplace cities for
Inglewood residents are Los Angeles, Inglewood, Culver City, Santa Monica, and Torrance, as
shown on Figure 6-1, Job Counts by Work Place. Most Inglewood workers are employed in the City
of Los Angeles, potentially signaling greater morning commute traffic flows on I-405 North, I-105
East, and I-110 North.

6.4 Roadway Network
6.4.1 Roadway Classification
An important component of the mobility system is the roadway network, which has a typology
classification system for understanding how each type of roadway functions, also known as
“functional classification.” Inglewood has five main roadway types: freeways, arterials (major and
minor arterials), collectors, and local streets. The classifications typically align with the number of
lanes, the type of service the roadway intends to provide, and the existing use and location of
each roadway. The roadway typologies primarily focus on providing access for vehicles.

Page 6-8  CITY OF INGLEWOOD | EXISTING CONDITIONS REPORT | January 2025
   Chapter 6 Circulation

Freeways. Freeways provide intercity and regional travel, and they can accommodate the highest
traffic volumes. All planning, design, and improvements of freeways are under the jurisdiction of
Caltrans. Two freeways fall within the City of Inglewood boundaries:

•  Interstate 405 (I-405) serves as a north-south route in the Inglewood area. It averages six
  travel lanes in each direction and carries an average of 379,000 vehicles per day.

•  Interstate 105 (I-105) serves as an east-west route along the south edge of Inglewood. There
  are six travel lanes going west toward LAX and five travel lanes going east. During peak
  commute hours, the corridor experiences demand that exceeds the freeway’s capacity at
  200,000 to 250,000 vehicles per day.

Arterials. Arterial roadways are designed to carry high volumes of motorized traffic. Arterial
roadways in Inglewood are classified as Major Arterials and Minor Arterials. Although similar in
functionality, Minor Arterials have lower speeds and cover smaller geographic areas compared to
Major Arterials.

•  Major Arterials. Major arterials function as primary intercity routes (i.e. continuous routes
  into, through, and out of the city) in addition to collecting and distributing a large portion of
  local traffic. They are designed to carry over 10,000 vehicles per day and have at least two
  travel lanes in each direction. Examples of major arterials in the city include La Cienega
  Boulevard, La Brea Avenue, Imperial Highway, and Manchester Boulevard.

•  Minor Arterials. Minor Arterials may be discontinuous within the city, carry less traffic volume,
  and/or serve as extensions of other major arterials. They are typically designed to carry 3,000
  to 10,000 vehicles per day and have at least two travel lanes in each direction. Crenshaw Drive,
  Overhill Drive, and Van Ness Avenue are some examples.

Collectors. Collectors are transitional roadways that connect local roads and streets with arterials.
The function of a collector is to “collect” vehicles from the local street system and transport them
to the arterial system. Collectors may be designed to carry up to 15,000 vehicles per day, although
many typically accommodate 3,000 to 10,000 vehicles. A collector roadway will have at least one
travel lane in each direction, but depending on specific traffic volume or access function, it may
have two travel lanes in each direction. Hyde Park Boulevard, 104th Steet, and Beach Avenue are
some collector streets in Inglewood.

Local Roads. Local roads are the most common type in the roadway network. In most of the city,
they connect directly to local residences and other destinations that are not served by other
roadway types.

In the five-year period between 2019 and 2023, the city had 1,919 vehicular collisions. Of these,

6.5 Transit System
Transit is an important part of the mobility network. It expands transportation options to those
who may not be able to afford or physically operate other means of travel and to those who prefer
it over driving.

6.5.1 Transit Operations and Programs
Transit service in Inglewood is currently served by multiple agencies and programs, as detailed in
Table 6-3. With nine bus lines, LA Metro is the biggest provider of fixed-route buses throughout
the city. LA Metro also has three light-rail stations within the city boundaries. The recently
completed K line created the Westchester/Veterans Station, Downtown Inglewood Station, and
Fairview Heights Station. Also, the Crenshaw Station along the C Line is on the southern edge in
Hawthorne but provides services to city residents. Other transit operators include Torrance Transit,
which has one fixed route, and the Link-Lennox and Link-Athens, which are operated by Los
Angeles County to serve the Lennox and Athens communities but have stops in Inglewood.

In addition to transit operators, several programs offer transit services in the city. The I Line Shuttle,
offered by the Inglewood Senior Center, is a fixed route that has 25 stops across the city. Iride
Inglewood is a point-to-point-based service for residents traveling between LAX and the
Inglewood/Lennox area. It is a collaborative program between the City of Inglewood and Los
Angeles World Airports. On game days, Torrance Transit has extra operations to SoFi stadium
from the Mary K. Giordano Regional Transit Center, and SoFI stadium offers a shuttle service from
the LA Metro C Line Hawthorne/Lennox Station. Intuit Dome provides a micro transit shuttle for
visitors within a six-mile radius and a regional park & ride service from five designated locations
across Los Angeles County.

6.6.2 Bicycle Infrastructure
Bicycling is a low-cost transportation mode that allows travelers to reach destinations further than
by walking alone. Bicycling infrastructure contains two main components: the bikeway network
and bicycle amenities such as parking and end-of trip amenities.

Bikeway Network
Similar to the functional classification typology for roadways, there are several types of bikeways
in the bikeway network.

•  Bike Paths (Class I Bikeways). Paved facilities for the exclusive use of bicyclists, pedestrians,
  and other non- motorized travel modes.

•  Bike Lanes (Class II Bikeways). On-street lanes reserved for the exclusive use of bicyclists.
  Colored pavement may be added to increase visibility of the facility, identify conflict areas and
  reinforce priority to bicyclists in conflict areas.

•  Buffered Bike Lanes. Conventional bike lanes with a designated buffer space separating the
  bike lane from the adjacent motor vehicle lane and/or parking lane. Colored pavement may
  be added.

•  Bike Routes (Class III Bikeways). Travel routes for bicyclists on which a separate lane or path
  is either not feasible or not desirable. Bicyclists and cars share lanes on bike routes (typically
  the rightmost lane).

•  Bike Boulevards. Streets with low motorized traffic volumes at low speeds, designated and
  design to give bicycle travel priority. Like bike routes, bicyclists and cars share the same lanes.

•  Protected Bike Lanes (Class IV Bikeways). Bike lanes with a physical barrier between the
  bike lane and other travel/parking lanes. Protected bike lane treatments may be one-way
  facilities or two-way facilities. Colored pavement may be added.
According to the AT SRTS Plan, the city has 3.2 miles of bikeways. Of these, 1.5 miles are Class II
bike lanes and 1.7 miles are Class III bike routes. These bikeways are generally routed along
Florence Avenue and South Van Ness Avenue. The City’s existing bikeways are depicted on Figure

6.12  Mobility Technologies
From ITS to electric vehicles, autonomous vehicles, and ride hailing services, technology is
changing the way people move. Further developments and innovations have the potential to
make travel safer, more convenient, and more environmentally sustainable, while bringing
unforeseen challenges. This section covers some of the new technologies to consider in planning
for mobility through 2050.

6.12.1 Intelligent Transportation Systems
Intelligent Transportation Systems integrate communication technologies with transportation
infrastructure and vehicles to improve safety and mobility. ITS encompasses a range of
technologies that are employed in a variety of ways to address many transportation challenges.
One example of ITS is Connected Vehicle technologies, which include V2V Communication and
V2I Communication. According to the US Department of Transportation, Connected Vehicle
technologies use V2X (vehicle to everything) communications for short-range broadcasts,
allowing vehicles to “sense” what other travelers are doing and identify potential hazards. This
technology could communicate with anything or anyone (such as a pedestrian or bicyclist) to help
reduce roadway collisions. Vehicle-to-vehicle communications (V2V) allow vehicles to “talk” with
each other. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, V2V communications
allow vehicles to be continuously aware of each other. One application is warning vehicles behind
another vehicle of sudden maneuvers, so they could slow down. Vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I)
communications, on the other hand, enable vehicles to communicate with the roadway
infrastructure. For example, emergency vehicles could “talk” with the City’s traffic operations
infrastructure and interrupt normal traffic signal timing to allow for green lights. This would allow
emergency responders to arrive more quickly at their intended destinations.

The City of Inglewood operates an ITS traffic management center through the Transportation
Division. In August 2024, the City approved an agreement with LA Metro to become a member of
the Regional Integration of Intelligent Transportation System (RIITS). Membership allows the city
to have access to members’ transportation data. And the transportation data collected from the
city, such as real-time traffic, transit, video, and other data relating to all modes of transportation,
will be shared with all members for transportation purposes. However, technologies for ITS are
constantly-evolving, and it is important for the City to continuously invest in the new technologies
to provide for a safer and more efficient transportation system.

6.12.2 Transportation Network Companies
Transportation network companies (TNC), such as Uber and Lyft, combine web-based
applications, such as mobile applications, and ridesharing vehicles. While TNCs could reduce
private vehicle ownership levels, they are also likely to increase total vehicle miles traveled. The
greatest factors that TNCs will affect in cities include parking, curb-space management, and transit
use—especially in areas where parking is currently considered “difficult.”

When people use TNC services in place of a privately owned automobile, the demand for parking
goes down, and the demand for curbside drop-off and pick-up locations rises. As TNCs continue
to rise and capture a greater share of travel modes, the City will have to identify areas where it is
difficult to park and develop strategies for curb space management, while reconsidering minimum
parking requirements. Minimum parking requirements may be reduced or eliminated or maximum
parking requirements could be introduced in specific areas of the city.

TNCs can help improve first-last mile connections, where a person must find transportation
options to get to a transit station, and from transit to their destination. The General Plan Update
should consider appropriate curbside management strategies, such as areas that either prioritize
or restrict passenger loading and unloading, as well as safety.

6.12.3 Electric Vehicles
Adoption of electric vehicles is becoming more widespread, with California transitioning to clean
energy vehicles by 2035. As a part of the Advanced Clean Cars II regulations, all new passenger
cars, trucks, and SUVs sold in the state are required to be zero-emission vehicles in 2035. In this
space, there could be an opportunity to create wireless charging areas for cars, bikes, microtransit,
and other mobility options that can charge in these areas.

To prepare for this new reality, the City would need to plan for more electric vehicle charging
areas and promote EV infrastructure in buildings. As the City considers potentials retrofits of
parking areas or develops roadways, it may want to consider this potential future and incorporate
specific elements to make implementation easier once an integrated platform is developed.

6.12.4 Autonomous Vehicles
Autonomous vehicles (AV) have the potential to revolutionize mobility. There are several levels of
vehicle autonomy. They range from cruise control (low level of autonomy) to fully autonomous
vehicles that require no interaction with the driver. It is unknown how long it will take to convert
all cars to AVs or if that will ever happen. However, the expansion of AVs will likely alter travel
behavior in the city. AVs are expected to make car travel less stressful, increase travel safety, and
reduce operational inefficiencies on freeways, all leading to an increase in demand for automobile
travel and potential farther expansion of land uses. The transition period, when streets carry large
numbers of both conventional and autonomous vehicles, will involve complex interactions and
require new informed analysis methods and professional judgment to address conflicts and
benefits.

Parking utilization will be altered by the introduction of AVs. In the United States, a considerable
amount of land is dedicated to parking by way of minimum parking requirements. Today there
are about five parking spaces per vehicle in the United States; however, in the future as more
shared AVs are available, the need for parking would likely be reduced. The General Plan would
need to include strategies that anticipate how these changes in parking and the future AV fleet
could affect the City’s mobility system.

6.12.5 Microtransit
Microtransit is technology-enabled, demand-responsive transit service that is open to everyone.
It can be used as incremental improvement to coverage-oriented dial-a-ride or paratransit
services by suburban transit agencies, as a supplement of low-performing suburban fixed route
services by transit agencies, or as a premium for-profit fixed route service interlining with already
overcapacity urban transit corridors. When considering a new service, a fixed-route bus is likely to
best accomplish a ridership goal, and microtransit is better suited to a coverage goal that
complements existing fixed-route transit service.

6.12.6 Solar Roadway Technology
Solar roadway is a technological advancement that is currently being researched by agencies such
as the Federal Highway Administration for the purpose of providing charging for electrical
vehicles. Solar panel cells are embedded into the roadway to harvest solar radiation into
renewable energy. The surface of the solar cells is laminated in glass and light-emitting diodes.
Solar technology still has a way to go. There are still constraints to work through, such as surface
friction, water infiltration, cost of construction/maintenance, and lower than expected energy
returns.

6.13.2 Implications for Planning
The City’s mobility system supports a variety of functions, and it is constantly transforming. Growth
in the city will change how people move around, resulting in new circulation-related challenges
and opportunities. The state-of-practice of transportation planning is also dynamic. It has
transformed since adoption of the current general plan, shaped by new legislation, appreciation
of the relationship between transportation and climate change, and resulting design paradigms.

The General Plan Update process is an opportunity for Inglewood to consider the existing mobility
landscape and develop a responsive, forward-thinking set of transportation goals and policies.
These policies will enable the City’s transportation infrastructure and system to adapt to future
development and ensure sustainability, resiliency, and equity. Based on the existing conditions
assessment in this document, key topics to consider in this new transportation planning and policy
framework follow.

Establishment of local transportation priorities. The past decade has seen significant shifts in
how mobility projects are prioritized, assessed, and regulated. The change from LOS to VMT and
focus on collision reduction are just two examples of this. Given Inglewood’s recent history of new
and proposed projects, the City may benefit from adopting a set of local transportation priorities
and evaluation guidelines. The process could consider standards such as VMT reduction,
facilitation of active modes, climate friendliness, fatality reduction rates and others. The resulting
framework would not supplant required review such as CEQA, but help the City formally evaluate
potential projects and responses to local mobility deficiencies.

“Complete” transportation corridors and multimodal urban design. Many of the City’s
commercial land uses are located along major transportation corridors. These corridors are auto-
oriented, and their design separates businesses from either side and creates unpleasant public
realms. Better design of public streets that complement existing land uses can create new public
spaces that people can enjoy while supporting local businesses.

Planning for mobility hubs. Mobility hubs are nodes where multiple transportation options and
modes are available for travelers to connect to their destinations. Mobility hubs can be microlocal
spaces with a bus shelter, bike parking, and drop-off spaces for ridesharing, or regional in scale
with commuter rail integration, a bus transfer facility, transit plaza, bike repair station, ridesharing
pick-up, and microtransit. Mobility hubs help promote a more sustainable and equitable mobility
system by giving people alternative options for driving. This is vital in Inglewood, where a new
web of regional destinations and transit infrastructure continue to transform the circulation
landscape.

7.1.1 Water System Environmental Setting and Infrastructure

The City’s water utility department provides water to 86 percent of the residences and businesses
in Inglewood. The City’s water service area comprises 4,608 acres, or approximately 78 percent of
the city’s total area of 5,825 acres. Approximately 45 percent of the land use in the City’s water

7.1.4 Existing Water Capacity Assessment and Water Planning
City of Inglewood 2015 Water Master Plan
In 2015, the City updated its Water Master Plan (WMP) to evaluate existing and future system
infrastructure and operations. The WMP provides a working document to assess infrastructure
and operation improvements to enable system reliability, redundancies, and efficiencies for a
20-year planning horizon with the water CIP, which was created for over 40 years to efficiently
fund recommended system improvements. The WMP utilizes the City’s General Plan Land Use
data available in 2015, which includes the Hollywood Park Specific Plan. A hydraulic model of the
City’s water system was developed to model system performance and pressures to assess
deficiencies and recommend improvements in the CIP. As part of the analysis, peak-hour demands
are calculated and modeled throughout the system to determine if there are any pressure
deficiencies throughout the water system and to confirm sufficient water supply for required
domestic and fire suppression scenarios. All system pressures were found to be above the
minimum-required operating pressure, and the system was deemed to be operating effectively.
Additionally, the system is tested to determine if it is capable of sustaining adequate fire flow
pressure (minimum 20 pounds per square inch (psi) for fire suppression scenario) per Los Angeles
County Fire Department requirements. As a result of the hydraulic analysis, a total of 350 fire-flow
deficiencies were identified at various deficiency levels. 6 These deficiencies are being addressed
in the City’s CIP for water system projects.

7.2.1 Sewer System
The City provides sewer service to the community through a collection system comprising
149 miles of gravity sewer pipes. Pipe diameters range from four to six inches for lateral lines and
eight to ten inches for sewer mains. The City’s system also consists of 3,246 manholes and does
not include any pump stations but is entirely gravity flow. The City is part of Los Angeles County
Sanitation Districts’ (LACSD) District No. 5. The majority of sewers tie directly into Los Angeles
LACSD trunk lines crossing the city primarily in arterial streets. LACSD trunk lines range from 10
to 24 inches in diameter. There are two LACSD-owned pumping stations in the city and
approximately 200 connections to LACSD trunk sewers, which send the city’s wastewater south to
LACSD’s A.K. Warren Water Resource Facility (Warren Facility) in the city of Carson for treatment
and disposal of wastewater. 7

The sewers are primarily constructed of vitrified clay pipe. Approximately 95 percent of the pipes
are eight inches in diameter. The majority of the existing sewer system was constructed before
1960. Figure 7-3 displays the City’s and LACSD’s existing sewer system facilities.

As previously mentioned, all wastewater flows from the City are sent to the Warren Facility. The

Drainage Facilities

The city is largely built out with a storm drain system consisting of catch basins and storm drain

Total Maximum Daily Loads

Once a water body has been listed as impaired on the 303(d) list, a TMDL for the relevant
pollutant(s) must be developed for that water body. A TMDL is an estimate of the daily load of
pollutants that a water body could receive from point sources, nonpoint sources, and natural
background conditions (including an appropriate margin of safety), without exceeding its water
quality standard. The facilities and activities that discharge into the water body must not,
collectively, exceed the TMDL. In general terms, MS4s and other dischargers within each
watershed are collectively responsible for meeting the required reductions and other TMDL
requirements by the assigned deadline.

Identifying water quality priorities is a main component of the EWMP process because the MS4
Permit requires that water quality characterization, water body pollutants, and source assessments
be prioritized. The MS4 Permit describes three categories of priority:

•  Category 1: Highest Priority
  - Water body pollutants with an established TMDL in the MS4 Permit.

•  Category 2: High Priority
  - Pollutants that indicate water quality impairment according to the State’s Water Quality
  Control Policy 303(d) list and MS4 discharges that could be contributing to water quality
  impairment.

•  Category 3: Medium Priority
  - Pollutants that have exceeded applicable receiving water limitations in the MS4 Permit but
  have insufficient data to indicate they contribute to water quality impairment or
  exceedance in the receiving water(s).

Groundwater Conditions

The city lies within the Coastal Plain of Los Angeles Groundwater Basin and specifically under the
adjudicated West Coast Groundwater Subbasin (West Coast Basin) and Central Groundwater
Subbasin (Central Basin), as depicted on Figure 7-6 18 The Water Replenishment District of
Southern California (WRD) is responsible for maintaining and replenishing both the West Coast
Basin and Central Basin. To maintain groundwater quality, WRD conducts an extensive monitoring
program that serves and manages each basin’s groundwater production, contamination, and
compliance with all required laws and regulations. Additionally, to ensure accurate data, WRD uses
depth-specific (nested) monitoring wells that tap discrete aquifer zones. In the most recent
Regional Groundwater Monitoring Report, 19 WRD presents water quality results from the 22 WRD
nested monitoring wells (112 individual wells zones) during the 2022-2023 water year. WRD
collected hundreds of samples from these wells and concluded that groundwater in its service
area is of generally good quality and suitable for use, noting that any localized areas with marginal
to poor water quality can be treated and utilized as potable water.

Sustainable Groundwater Management Act
The California Sustainable Groundwater Management Act is a three-bill package signed into law
in 2014 that creates a framework for the management of groundwater sources throughout the
state. Under the act, local agencies form groundwater sustainability agencies and create
groundwater sustainability plans for basins designated as high and medium priority. Other than
annual reporting, the act does not apply to existing adjudicated areas, such as the West Coast and
Central Basin, because they have existing court-mandated governance, oversight, and
management in place. Furthermore, local agencies in low- or very-low-priority basins, like the
West Coast Basin and Central Basin, are not required to form groundwater sustainability agencies
or develop groundwater sustainability plans, but may do so voluntarily. They may also develop
groundwater management plans to actively manage their groundwater resources, as noted
previously with the Los Angeles RWQCB’s Basin Management Plan.

7.4 Findings
7.4.1 Community Outreach Feedback
During the outreach activities conducted by the project team, several comments were provided
by stakeholders on the city’s wet infrastructure. Commenters expressed a desire for water
conservation activities, including rainwater capture, the reuse of water, and the planting of native
species that are drought tolerant and are less reliant on water use. A desire to improve the quality
of the city’s drinking water was also expressed.

7.4.2 Implications for Planning
Water

Overall, water demands within the city have been estimated at 9,132 AFY for the City’s water utility
department as of 2020. Existing water demands for the remaining 14 percent of the City serviced
by GSWC Southwest and CAWC are unavailable. As shown in the City’s 2015 WMP, the water
infrastructure system effectively conveys these demands. The overall distribution system was
found to be in good condition, and the Master Plan identifies several capital improvement projects
and recommendations to address any current or projected water system deficiencies.
Groundwater and imported water are the supply sources for all three water purveyors. Each water
purveyor pumps groundwater from either the West Coast or Central Subbasin and purchases
imported water through Metropolitan Water District connections.

Wastewater

Overall, existing sewer flows have been estimated through the City’s 2017 Sewer Master Plan at
an average flow of 0.273 million gallons per day (mgd) and peak flow of 0.546 mgd. The existing
sewer infrastructure system effectively convey these existing flows, but some deficiencies exist.
The City has CIP programs in place to address deficiencies in the City’s sewer system.

Stormwater and Water Quality

In summary, storm drainage throughout the city is conveyed via local catch basins and storm drain
facilities that are owned and maintained by the City, LACFCD, and Caltrans. Local storm drain
facilities convey flows to LACFCD regional storm drain facilities. These facilities tend to be large-
diameter pipes, reinforced concrete boxes, and trapezoidal flood control channels.

8.1.2 Park Need
Park need is traditionally measured with a single metric, such as the number of acres of parkland
available to residents, or the percentage of residents living within walking distance of a park.

The City’s 1995 Open Space Element “encourages” the City to reestablish its 1970 parkland-to-
population ratio of 1 acre of park space per 1,000 residents. At present, 89.6 acres of the city are
utilized as parkland. With its current population of 102,865 persons, the city would require 103
acres of parkland to meet this 1 acre per 1,000 residents ratio.

The 1995 Open Space Element applied a 1-mile service radius for Edward Vincent Park, given its
status of a Large Park. A 0.5-mile radius was applied to medium size parks (typically about 10
acres); and a 0.33-mile radius was applied to small parks under 2 acres. Using these service radii,

per 1,000 residents. Finally, Culver City’s service standard aims to provide 10 acres of park space
per 1,000 residents, with 1 acre per 1,000 residents able to be satisfied with joint use agreements
with the local school district and another 6 acres per 1,000 residents able to be satisfied by
regional parks.

Regional Parks

The appropriate distance to a park varies depending on the size and purpose of the park. Regional
Parks may attract visitors within an hour’s drive time. By comparison, the Los Angeles County 2022
Comprehensive Parks and Recreation Needs Assessment+ utilizes a 0.5-mile walking and a 2.5-
mile cycling distance to regional recreation areas, calculated along the walkable road/pedestrian
network. Other forms of access are calculated through a 5-mile driving radius, as well as public
transit stops within 0.5 mile of a park entrance.

The nearest Regional Recreation Park to Inglewood is the Kenneth Hahn State Recreation Area.
This Recreation Area is 401 acres in size, and its southeastern entrance is approximately 1.07 miles
from Inglewood’s northern boundary. The presence of this Recreation Area increases
northwestern Inglewood’s access to parkland.

8.1.3 Park Sustainability
Parkland sustainability can be achieved through multiple methods. For instance, Lake Park
provides 12 acres of privately owned public open space in Inglewood immediately south of SoFi
Stadium. Lake Park features several sustainable park practices, such as Southern California native
plant species. By using plant species from California’s biogeographic zones, such as desert flora,
low-elevation chaparral, and riparian ecosystems, the overall water demand for the site is lessened.
This use of native plants also encourages the return of native wildlife. The centerpiece of Lake Park
is the six-acre Rivers Lake. Rivers Lake functions as a water recycling system by collecting
stormwater runoff from its surroundings and filtering it through natural wetlands and mechanical
systems, which are then used to irrigate Lake Park.

IUSD has experienced declining enrollment over the past ten years, from an enrollment of 10,959
students during the 2014/15 school year to 6,958 students in the 2023/2024 school year.

IUSD projected a declining enrollment over the next six years, with a projected 5,476 students in
the 2029/30 school year. This is a total decline of 1,482 students from the current school year, a
decrease of 21.3%. Based on current IUSD standards for classroom space, the District has a net
classroom capacity of 12,293 students. This gives the District a current utilization factor of 56.6%.
The projected utilization factor in 2029/2030 will be 44.5%.

IUSD has been in State Receivership since 2012, when the State of California loaned IUSD $29
million. Since then, IUSD has been making the required annual debt payments of approximately
$1.8 million each year. As of 2024, the outstanding loan balance was $21 million. Additionally,
receivership status requires the District to pay $410,000 for an annual comprehensive review by
the State-appointed Financial Crisis & Management Assistance Team (FCMAT). This annual review
measures IUSD progress on 155 standards. To exit receivership, IUSD is required to meet a
minimum score on all 155 standards that FCMAT reviews each year. This leads to a total payment
of $2,210,000 each year.

Due to declining enrollment, the cost of payments, and increased operating costs (due to the age
of IUSD facilities), IUSD has decided to close the following schools:

•  Crozier Junior High. For the 2024-25 school year, Crozier will not accept incoming 7th grade
  students. For the 2025-26 school year, Crozier will remain open as an 8th grade only school.
  The phased closure of Crozier will allow current 7th grade students to complete their 8th grade
  year at Crozier.

•  Hudnall Elementary School (Transitional Kindergarten–Grade 6). Hudnall is planned for closure
  at the end of the 2024-25 school year. Hudnall is one of three schools in the District that does
  not offer a TK-8 program.

•  Highland TK-6 School. Highland is planned for closure at the end of the 2024-25 school year.
  Highland is one of three schools in the District that does not offer a TK-8 program.

•  Morningside High School. Morningside High is planned for closure at the end of the 2024-25
  school year. The District reports that it is not possible to provide a comprehensive high school
  program with such a small student body. Extremely low enrollment results in limited course
  offerings and limited extracurricular and enrichment opportunities for students.

•  Kelso Elementary School (TK-6). Kelso is planned for closure at the end of the 2024-25 school
  year. Students and staff will move to the Daniel Freeman Warren Lane site, which will be re-
  opened as a TK-8 school. Kelso is one of three schools in the District that does not offer a TK-
  8 program.

These changes will allow all IUSD primary schools to serve children from Transitional Kindergarten
through 8th grade (TK-8).

8.3.3 Private and Charter Schools
A private school is a private business or nonprofit entity that offers or conducts full-time
instruction with a full complement of subjects at the elementary, middle, or high school level.
Private schools function outside the jurisdiction of the California Department of Education (CDE)
and most state education regulations. Private schools do not participate in California’s educational
accountability system and are directly accountable to students and their parents or guardians,
based on the terms of the private school enrollment contract. Private schools offer a range of
educational services for their students and have their own admission standards, curricula, and
graduation requirements.

Existing Programs and Services

The following programs increase public awareness of the police department’s activities:

•  National Night Out is an annual community-building campaign that promotes police-
  community partnerships and neighborhood camaraderie to make our neighborhoods safer
  and more caring places to live. It enhances the relationship between neighbors and law
  enforcement while restoring a true sense of community. Furthermore, it provides a great
  opportunity to bring police and neighbors together under positive circumstances.

•  Coffee with a Cop brings police officers and the community members they serve together over
  coffee to discuss issues and learn more about each other.

•  The Community Police Academy is a 10-week program designed to familiarize Inglewood
  residents and merchants with the inner workings of the Police Department. Many of the
  graduates go on to be volunteers for the Police Department.

•  Neighborhood Watch (Block Clubs) have been the primary component of crime prevention
  strategies. Neighbors are encouraged to organize and to look after one another. Block clubs
  are formed as a mechanism that permits residents to actively participate in safeguarding their
  neighborhoods.

•  The Inglewood Police Department's social media presence fosters communication,
  transparency, and community engagement. Through platforms like Facebook, Twitter, and
  Instagram, the department educates the public on safety tips and promotes community events
  to enhance public knowledge and involvement. Recognizing community contributions and
  supporting recruitment further strengthens the department's public image. Overall, the
  Inglewood Police Department's social media efforts are integral to maintaining a collaborative
  and informed relationship with the community.

Response Times and Protocol

LA County Fire uses the national guideline of a 5-minute response time for basic life support for
the first-arriving unit and an 8-minute response time for advanced life support (paramedic) in
urban areas as response time goals. In 2023, the average response time for the first-in-response
unit in Inglewood was 3:51 minutes/seconds.

LA County Fire notes that fire protection serving the Inglewood area is adequate with existing
development and land use. However, each additional development increases demands on existing
resources. Currently, LA County Fire has no plans for any service improvements or new facilities in
Inglewood. Though there are no studies or reports demonstrating rates of fire incidence
throughout Inglewood, LA County Fire has an online reporting system that generates ad hoc fire
incident reports, which allows the public to provide LA County Fire with customized reports based
on the incident witnessed. Once filed, these reports are available from the County of Los Angeles
Fire Department Public Records Office approximately two weeks after the date that the incident
occurred.

LA County Fire’s Prevention Division is under the command of an assistant fire chief designated
as the department’s fire marshal. The division focuses on educating the community about the
benefits of proper safety practices and identifying and eliminating all types of hazardous
conditions that pose a threat to life, the environment, and property.

8.6 Findings
8.6.1 Public Comments
This section summaries initial public feedback on public services and facilities gathered from the
engagement activities described in Chapter 1. The comments provide insight into community
perceptions of what is missing, what needs improvement, and what is currently working well in
Inglewood, guiding future planning considerations.

What People Appreciate about the City

In general, commenters appreciated the City’s existing parks and the programming available at
the City’s parks and community facilities, such as the senior center. With regard to parks,
commenters appreciated their safety and cleanliness. Commenters also appreciated special events
held in the city, such as fairs and festivals.

Missing / Need More of in the City

Commenters also stated that the City needed additional parks as well as specific facilities such as
teen centers, children’s programming, skate parks, and dog parks. Commenters also expressed a
desire for more trees in public spaces. Commenters sought additional upkeep of the City’s existing
parks and recreational facilities as well as increased safety and more security. Finally, commenters
wanted more art and events that reflected the city’s culture and values.

Needs to Improve

Commenters stated an overall need for maintaining and cleaning the city’s existing public spaces,
with litter removal being a key issue. Commenters expressed a desire for better advertising of the
City’s existing programs as well as more programs overall for a variety of age groups. Commenters
stated that the noise level in the city could be reduced, especially given the number of events held
at the city’s stadiums. Commenters also specifically called out that the city’s schools needed
improvements, especially in light of recent school closures.

Vision for the City

In their vision for the city, commenters expressed a desire for more parks and more public art,
well maintained, kept clean, and programmed with key features such as community events,
community gardens, cultural centers, sports courts, skate parks, and splash zones. Commenters
wanted a system of trails and paths connecting these public places in the city. They also spoke of
a desire to be part of an informed community whose culture has been preserved.

8.6.2 Implications for Planning
Parks and Recreation
As the General Plan Update evolves, there will be opportunities to confirm and elaborate on
existing plans and programs to address park needs and meet the City’s parkland goals. The
following opportunities should be explored further as updated policies and programs are defined.

•  Integrate privately owned public open spaces, such as the 12-acre Lake Park at SoFi Stadium,
  into new developments.

•  Increase open space standards for new residential development.

•  Require a dedication of land or payment of fees for all new residential development so that
  the City can acquire new land for parks in underserved areas or improve facilities at existing
  parks.

•  Formalize a joint-use agreement with Inglewood Unified School District to utilize existing
  schools as parks when school is not in session.

•  Explore utilizing former schools that have closed due to lack of enrollment (or portions
  thereof) as new parkland.

•  Incorporate sustainability features into parks to mitigate environmental impacts and reduce
  operating costs associated with water usage and electricity usage.

Library Facilities

As the City’s existing libraries facilities continue to age, new or renovated facilities may be
required. As previously stated, a new library is proposed as part of a new civic center facility. The
new library design accounts for community needs based on current population. Additional library
resources and updated collections may be required as the city’s population changes over time. In
addition, there may be a need for greater digital access at the City’s libraries, as resources such as
physical books are replaced by e-books, audiobooks, and other digital resources. Libraries also
are undergoing a shift in their role in the community, with libraries taking on more functions
traditionally served by community centers. The design and features of any new or renovated
library facilities in the city will need to take such functions into account.

Schools
The decline of the school-age population in Inglewood will lead to a significant decrease in the
number of students enrolled at IUSD in the near future and require significant changes to school
facilities and usage. While the projected utilization for IUSD’s facilities is expected to decline to
44.5% by 2030, utilization of IUSD’s existing facilities as more specialized spaces may allow IUSD
to provide a project-based learning model without significant new infrastructure. The closure of
school facilities may provide opportunities to consider how those grounds can best serve the
community in different ways in the future.

Police Services

As the City’s population and employment growth increases, the need for police services is
expected to grow due to the increase in population and workers and the associated potential for
additional crime and accidents. If increases in population employment lead to increased traffic
congestion, response times could drop below the target goal established by the Police
Department. If calls for service increase and exceed the capacity of Inglewood’s Police Department
existing workforce, additional staff would be needed and ongoing revenue would be needed to
fund additional staff.

Fire Services

Future development in the city can be expected to increase the need for new fire facilities,
apparatus, and personnel to maintain adequate response times. As discussed above, new
construction projects are required to pay fire facilities fees through engineering and building plan
reviews, as well as parcel and tract map plan reviews that contribute to the County’s funding to
acquire, construct, and furnish new fire protection and emergency services facilities and to
purchase new equipment.

9.1 Introduction
This chapter discusses the existing conditions and planning considerations related to the natural

9.2 Biological Resources
The City of Inglewood is entirely developed with urban uses and has limited presence of natural
biological resources. This section offers a discussion of those resources and the city’s natural
setting, which can influence the General Plan’s land uses and policy approach. This overview
focuses on resources in the city that characterize Inglewood's natural landscape.

9.2.1 Habitat Linkages and Corridors
Because the City is developed and urbanized with no open space connections, habitat linkages
and corridors are not present in Inglewood, according to the CFDW’s Biogeographic Information
and Observation System (BIOS). 1

9.2.2 Special-Status Plants and Wildlife
Plant communities and habitats in Inglewood are limited due to extensive urbanization and
development. Plant communities in urbanized areas typically consist of maintained ornamental
species. Special-status plants are those classified as rare or listed, proposed, or candidates for
threatened or endangered status under federal or California regulations. Special-status species
that have the potential to occur in the city are discussed in this section. Future proposed projects
must ensure the avoidance of disruption to endangered species.

Federal Endangered Species Act

The Federal Endangered Species Act of 1973 (FESA) defines an endangered species as “any species
that is in danger of extinction throughout all or a significant portion of its range.” Threatened
species are defined as “any species which is likely to become an endangered species within the

Inglewood. Climate change is a pressing and ongoing issue, intensifying various environmental
and public health challenges, including the urban heat island effect, increased frequency and
severity of heatwaves, heightened wildfire risks, and exacerbated flooding. These changes can
significantly impact urban infrastructure, ecosystems, and the well-being of residents.

Increased intensity and instances of the urban heat island effect can lead to greater occurrences
of heat-related illnesses and mortality. The combination of increased temperatures and
urbanization can result in more frequent and severe heatwaves. 6 Climate change can increase the

9.3.1 Extreme Heat
The effects of extreme heat can be amplified in urban centers with high levels of development,
such as the City of Inglewood, with potential consequences for health and air quality. Urbanized
areas experience significantly higher temperatures than natural landscapes, creating “heat islands”
that emphasize the effects of temperature increases associated with climate change. Roads, paved
lots, and building materials reflect less solar energy and absorb more heat compared to natural
vegetation cover, resulting in daytime temperatures in urban areas about 1°F to 7°F higher than
temperatures in outlying areas and nighttime temperatures about 2°F to 5°F higher. 8

As described in the 2022 Safety Element of the Inglewood General Plan, the intensity and duration
of extreme heat events has been increasing in the city. Average minimum temperatures and
annual number of extreme heat instances are expected to increase even more significantly in
upcoming years. 9 According to the EPA’s Environmental Justice Screening Tool, Inglewood had
less than 20 average days over 90ºF per census block (from 2019 to 2023).

Extreme Heat Mitigation Measures
To address extreme heat in Inglewood, the General Plan Safety Element outlines several goals
aimed at mitigating its impact on residents and infrastructure. Implementation S-3.2.5 proposes
reducing the urban heat island effect by introducing cooling features in neighborhoods, such as
cool pavement materials, cool corridors, and innovative designs to enhance pedestrian comfort
at public transit stops and park amenities. Additionally, it recommends establishing cooling spaces
like open areas and cooling centers. Implementation S-3.2.6 focuses on adopting development
standards that incorporate climate-adapted urban design principles, especially in high-heat areas
and for vulnerable populations, such as seniors or multi-family housing. These standards may
include cross-ventilation, increased open space, use of cool materials, green roofing, and
requirements for both heating and cooling systems in buildings.

Shade and Tree Canopy Cover
Increasing tree canopy cover and vegetation in urban spaces can significantly mitigate the effects
of extreme heat. Expanding the tree canopy and adding greenery in urban areas helps reduce the
urban heat island effect. Research shows that urban forests can lower sensible heat flux and
increase latent heat flux, resulting in cooler surroundings. Strategically planting trees—such as
around buildings or to shade pavements in parking lots and streets—can enhance their
effectiveness in mitigating extreme heat. 11

Observed temperatures during extreme heat events vary significantly across Inglewood due to
differences in housing density, impervious surfaces, building type, and presence of tree canopy.
As of 2015, the city had an average tree canopy cover of 14 percent that ranged from 6 to 20
percent across Inglewood. Much of the existing canopy cover consists of smaller ornamental trees,
such as palms, instead of larger shade trees, such as oaks. Low-income neighborhoods also
contain disproportionately less tree shade and natural land surface cover, contributing to higher
temperatures during extreme heat events.12

9.3.3 Flooding
Climate change intensifies rainfall by increasing atmospheric moisture levels, as warmer
temperatures enhance the atmosphere’s capacity to hold water vapor. This elevated moisture
contributes to more intense and frequent extreme precipitation events when the additional water
vapor is released during storms, leading to heavier and more intense rainfall. 17 Periods of intense
rainfall exacerbated by climate change can lead to increased urban flooding if urban storm drains
are not properly equipped to handle large amounts of water. In urbanized areas such as
Inglewood, direct runoff is extensive, not only because of the density of impermeable pavements,
which allow less rain to infiltrate the ground, but also because storm-sewer systems carry more
water directly to the ocean. The presence of vegetation and other natural surface cover absorbs
water and reduces the volume of runoff. 18

Because Inglewood is in the upper portion of the local Dominguez Channel watershed, the city is
not in the path of any upstream runoff and is not susceptible to flooding. According to FEMA,
Inglewood is in Zone X, an area of minimal flood hazard. In 1974, the Federal Insurance
Administration determined that the likelihood of flooding in Inglewood is less than 1 percent per
year.

Mobile Sources of Air Pollution

The other 80 percent of ozone-forming air pollution comes from mobile sources—mainly cars,
trucks, and buses, but also construction equipment, ships, trains, and airplanes. 22 Airports attract
a variety of mobile emissions sources, including private and commercial passenger vehicles,
shuttle and intercity buses, medium and heavy-duty trucks, private and commercial aircraft, and
a wide range of ground support equipment. The Federal Aviation Administration forecasts that
California aircraft activity will increase by two-thirds between now and 2050 based on historical
aircraft activity and economic predictors. Specifically, nitrogen oxides (NOX) emissions from
aircraft operations in California are projected to increase from 55 to 71 tons per day (tpd) between
2024 and 2050, whereas all other mobile source sectors are projected to decrease. 23
Consequently, in the Los Angeles metropolitan area, the combustion of gasoline and other
hydrocarbon fuels in airplanes contributes to various emitted pollutants. 24

Additionally, diesel engines emit diesel particulate matter (DPM) that contribute to cancer and
acute health risk in the Air Basin. 25 Almost all diesel exhaust particles are 10 microns or less in
diameter, and due to their extremely small size, these particles can be inhaled and eventually
trapped in the bronchial and alveolar regions of the lungs. Long-term (chronic) inhalation of DPM
is likely a lung cancer risk. Even short-term (i.e., acute) exposure can cause irritation and
inflammatory symptoms and may exacerbate existing allergies and asthma symptoms. 26

Most major sources of DPM emissions, such as ships, trains, and trucks, operate in and around
ports, rail yards, and heavily traveled roadways. These areas are often near highly populated areas,
which leads to elevated exposure to DPM levels in urban areas such as Inglewood.

9.4.2 Sensitive Receptors and Mitigation
Sensitive Receptors

Some land uses are considered more sensitive to air pollution than others due to the types of
population groups or activities involved. Sensitive population groups include children, the elderly,
the acutely ill, and the chronically ill, especially those with cardiorespiratory diseases. Residential
areas are also considered sensitive to air pollution because residents (including children and the
elderly) tend to be at home for extended periods of time, resulting in sustained exposure to any
pollutants present. Other sensitive receptors include retirement facilities, hospitals, daycare, and
schools.

Placement of New Sensitive Receptors

To reduce exposure to toxic air contaminants (TAC), CARB developed and approved the Air Quality
and Land Use Handbook: A Community Health Perspective (2005) to provide guidance regarding
the siting of sensitive land uses in the vicinity of freeways, distribution centers, rail yards, ports,
refineries, chrome-plating facilities, dry cleaners, and gasoline-dispensing facilities. 28 This
guidance document was developed to assess compatibility and associated health risks when siting
sensitive receptors near existing pollution sources. CARB’s recommendations were based on a
compilation of studies that evaluated data on the adverse health effects from proximity to air
pollution sources. The key observation in these studies was that proximity substantially increases
exposure and the potential for adverse health effects.

9.5.1 Regional and Local Faults and Seismicity
The city is in a seismically active region and faces a high probability of severe shaking due to an
earthquake about every thirty years. 36 Seismic ground shaking could damage buildings, parking
areas, and utility infrastructure in the city. Historically, two major earthquakes along the Newport-
Inglewood fault resulted in major damage and loss of life for communities on and around the
fault trace. On June 21, 1920, a magnitude 4.9 earthquake struck the communities surrounding
the fault, resulting in significant damage to existing infrastructure. This led to a better
understanding of the Newport-Inglewood fault, which helped in the development of measures to
protect the community along and around the fault. On March 10, 1933, a magnitude 6.4
earthquake hit the southern segment of the Newport-Inglewood Fault, which resulted in
widespread damage to the region and 115 to 200 deaths. Since then, modern infrastructure has
been developed to mitigate damage and potential loss of life to the communities in the region.
To mitigate any potential hazards related to seismic events, projects in the city are required to
conform with the City of Inglewood Department of Building and Safety building codes pertaining
to earthquake hazards and the 2022 California Building Code (CBC).

Faults and Seismicity
Alquist-Priolo Fault Zones are regulatory zones surrounding the surface traces of active faults.
Alquist-Priolo Fault Zones in and near the city include the Newport-Inglewood Fault, which is an
active fault line running through the city, and the Palos Verdes Fault, which runs west of the city. 37
Quaternary faults, which are typically small fissures in the earth’s crust and have moved within the
past 1.6 million years, also exist in and around the city, such as the Overland Avenue fault, and the
Charnock Fault. The City has experienced seismic events in the past from the mentioned
surrounding faults. Figure 9-9, Earthquake Faults, shows the location of major faults that cross the
City of Inglewood.

Regional and Local Faults

Newport-Inglewood Fault (Rose Canyon Fault Zone)
The Newport-Inglewood-Rose Canyon fault zone traverses the northwest part of the city,
including the Inglewood Park Cemetery. The fault zone consists of a series of northwest-trending,
generally right-lateral strike-slip faults. This fault zone is a major structural element, or major
geological structure that outlines different geologic units in the Peninsular Ranges, separating
contrasting Mesozoic basement terrane-Catalina Schist on the west and metasediments,
intrusives, and volcanics to the east. A Holocene to late Pleistocene age has been determined for
traces in the quadrangle, with a slip rate of about 1.0 millimeter/year. 38 This right-lateral fault zone
is composed of numerous fault splays that collectively can produce a magnitude 7.5 earthquake.

Overland Avenue Fault
The Overland Avenue Fault is a late Quaternary fault that nearly coincides with Overland Avenue
in Culver City; it is about six miles long and trends to the northwest, from the southwestern part
of the Baldwin Hills northwestward across Ballona Gap. This fault is located immediately north-
northwest of the city.

Charnock Fault
The Charnock Fault is a late Quaternary fault west of Inglewood. It is immediately west of the
Overland Avenue Fault and forms the western edge of the graben. The area between the two
faults has dropped as much as 140 feet during the Pliocene; however, the late Pleistocene and
Holocene sediments have not been displaced. Therefore, the faults are only considered potentially
active by the California Geological Survey.

Seismic Hazards

Liquefaction
Liquefaction refers to loose, saturated sand, or gravel deposits that lose their load-supporting
capability when subjected to intense shaking. Liquefaction potential varies based upon three main
contributing factors: 1) cohesionless, granular soils having relatively low densities (usually of
Holocene age); 2) shallow groundwater (generally less than 50 feet); and 3) moderate to high
seismic ground shaking. As described in the Safety Element, there is one Liquefaction Zone in the
northwest area of Inglewood, as shown on Figure 9-10. 39 Specifically, this area covers areas
surrounding Industrial Park Avenue and further along to West Hyde Park Boulevard and areas
north of West Florence Avenue. A small and localized section of this zone extends to the north,
just north of Centinela Avenue. The liquefaction zone continues east, north of Cable Way, with
coverage over Rogers Park, extending alongside West Florence Avenue and ending north-
northeast of Vincent Park, where a majority of Vincent Park’s central portion is located in a
liquefaction zone. 40

Landslides
Landsliding is a type of erosion in which masses of earth and rock move down slope as a single
unit. Susceptibility of slopes to landslides and other forms of slope failure depend on several
factors. These factors are usually present in combination and include steep slopes, condition of
rock and soil materials, the presence of water, formational contacts, geologic shear zones, and
seismic activity. Inglewood is mostly developed and flat. The only location having landslide
potential is in the Inglewood Park Cemetery. The remainder of the city is not susceptible to
landslides. 41

Inglewood sits atop the Coastal Plain of Los Angeles, with the majority of the city in Groundwater
Basin 4-011.03, and eastern parts of the territory in Groundwater Basin 4-011.04. They are
commonly referred to as the “West Coast Basin” and the “Central Basin,” respectively. See Figure
7-6 for their location.

West Coast Basin
The West Coast Basin is bounded on the north by the Ballona Escarpment, an abandoned
erosional channel from the Los Angeles River. It is bounded on the east by the Newport-
Inglewood fault zone. The basin is bounded on the south and west by the Pacific Ocean and
consolidated rocks of the Palos Verdes Hills. Discharge of groundwater from the basin occurs
primarily by pumping extractions. The Silverado aquifer, which underlies much of the West Coast
Basin, is the most productive aquifer in the region, supplying 80% to 90% of the basin's annual
groundwater extraction.

Recharge Areas
The natural replenishment of the Basin's groundwater supply is mainly restricted to underflow
from the Central Basin via the Newport-Inglewood fault zone. Water that infiltrates into the
aquifers of the Central Basin can eventually cross this fault and contribute to the groundwater
supply in the West Coast Basin.

The West Coast Basin receives minor replenishment through the infiltration of surface water from
the Los Angeles and San Gabriel Rivers into the uppermost aquifers. Additional minor recharge
sources include irrigation return flows from fields and lawns, industrial wastewater, and other
applied surface waters. 56

Central Basin
The Central Basin is bounded on the north by a surface divide called the La Brea high. The basin
is bounded on the northeast and east by rocks of the Elysian, Repetto, Merced and Puente Hills.
The southeastern boundary between the Central Basin and the Orange County Groundwater Basin
roughly aligns with Coyote Creek, which marks a regional drainage divide. The southwestern
boundary is defined by the Newport-Inglewood fault system and the folded rocks of the Newport-
Inglewood uplift.

The primary productive aquifers in the basin are the Gardena and Gage aquifers in the Lakewood
Formation and the Silverado, Lynwood, and Sunnyside aquifers in the San Pedro Formation.
Historically, groundwater in the Central Basin flowed from recharge areas in the northeast to the
Pacific Ocean in the southwest. However, increased pumping has lowered water levels in the
Central Basin, resulting in similar water levels on both sides of the Newport-Inglewood uplift and
reducing subsurface outflow to the West Coast Basin.

9.7 Noise and Vibration
9.7.1 Noise Fundamentals
Noise is defined as unwanted sound and is known to have several adverse effects on people who
are overexposed, including hearing loss, speech and sleep interference, physiological responses,
and annoyance. Although sound can be easily measured, the perception of noise and the physical
response to sound complicate the analysis of its impact on people. People judge the relative
magnitude of sound sensation in subjective terms such as “noisiness” or “loudness.”

Changes of 1 to 3 decibels (dBA)—the unitless measure of sound on a logarithmic scale—are
detectable under quiet, controlled conditions, and changes of less than 1 dBA are usually
indiscernible. A 3 dBA change in noise levels is considered the minimum change that is detectable
with human hearing in outside environments. A change of 5 dBA is readily discernable to most
people in an exterior environment, and a 10 dBA change is perceived as a doubling (or halving)
of the sound.

9.7.2 Vibration Fundamentals
Vibration is a trembling, quivering, or oscillating motion of the earth. Like noise, vibration is
transmitted in waves, but in this case through the earth or solid objects. Unlike noise, vibration is
typically of a frequency that is felt rather than heard.

Vibration can be either natural as in the form of earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, sea waves,
landslides, or man-made as from explosions, music frequencies, and the action of heavy
machinery or heavy vehicles such as trains. Both natural and man-made vibration may be
continuous such as from operating machinery, or transient as from an explosion.

9.7.3 Sensitive Receptors
Certain land uses, such as residences, schools, and hospitals, libraries, places of worship, and parks
are particularly sensitive to noise and vibration. These uses are regarded as sensitive because they
are where citizens most frequently engage in activities that are likely to be disturbed by noise,
such as reading, studying, sleeping, resting, or engaging in quiet or passive recreation.
Commercial and industrial uses are not particularly sensitive to noise or vibration.

9.7.4 Traffic Noise
On-road vehicles represent the most prominent source of noise in the city. Traffic noise levels
depend primarily on the speed of the traffic and the volume of trucks and are typically greatest
during peak traffic periods such as morning and evening commute times, and during major events
at entertainment facilities that draw many vehicles in a short period of time. The primary source
of vehicular noise from automobiles is high-frequency tire noise, which increases with speed.
Freeways that traverse Inglewood include I-405 along the western portion of the city and I-105 in
southern Inglewood, each having 250,000+ daily vehicles, resulting in noise levels of 76 dBA CNEL

influence area to disclose that fact to the person buying the property.

minimize public exposure to excessive noise and safety hazards, and the Commission’s Los

Mitigation Efforts

In public meetings for the Environmental Justice Element of the Inglewood General Plan, residents
identified aircraft noise from LAX as a major pollution concern for Inglewood. For the past several
decades, the Federal Aviation Administration and LAX have allocated over $400 million to the City
of Inglewood for purchasing, demolishing, or soundproofing hundreds of homes in noise contour

systems. The City's Residential Sound Insulation Department oversees these projects. Residents
are also urged to report excessive aircraft noise, short turns, low-flying aircrafts, and after-hour
arrivals (midnight to 6:30 a.m.) to Los Angeles World Airports Noise Management. 62

The Sound Insulation Grant Program, created by Los Angeles World Airports, is responsible for
administering and monitoring funds for various residential sound insulation (RSI) programs in
Inglewood. The Sound Insulation Grant Program also administers funding for sound insulation of
schools in the Inglewood Unified School District. The RSI programs, including the LAX RSI
Program, the Inglewood RSI Program, and the LA County RSI Program, are financed by grants
from Los Angeles World Airports and the Federal Aviation Administration. 63

Inglewood Residential Sound Insulation Program
The Inglewood RSI Program specifically serves residents of Inglewood. The program is for
homeowners whose properties (residential single family or multi-family) are within the Federal
Aviation Administration–Approved Part 150 Noise Exposure Map’s 65 dB noise contour. Eligible
homes must have been constructed before October 1, 1998, and be zoned for residential or
mixed-use purposes. Homes must have an average interior noise level (in habitable rooms) of 45
dB or higher.

Eligible homeowners will be contacted by RSI Program staff and introduced to the RSI Program.
Eligibility is confirmed through acoustical testing of the home using loudspeakers. An architectural
study and hazardous materials inspection will also take place prior to finalizing design plans. Once
the scope of work is approved, contractors will bid on the project and must meet the City’s

9.7.6 Light Rail Noise
The Metro K Line runs roughly parallel with Florence Avenue through the city with three stations,
Fairview Heights, Downtown Inglewood, and Westchester/Veterans. Noise-generating activities at
stations include entrance and egress from the stations (through stairways, escalators, and
elevators) as well as an increase in the number of people around the station. K Line service hours
are from 4:30 a.m. to 12:00 a.m. daily. Trains operate every 10 minutes throughout the day, and
night and early morning weekend service is every 20 minutes. According to the Federal Transit
Administration, noise levels from “rapid transit/light rail” range from 74 dBA to 80 dBA Lmax with
typical hourly noise levels of 63 dBA Leq at 50 feet.

Passing trains create vibration events that last approximately two minutes, though it is extremely
rare for vibration from train operations to cause substantial or even minor cosmetic building
damage. Older, historic buildings are often considered fragile and are the predominant source of
concern from rail-related vibration (FTA 2018). According to the Federal Transit Administration,
groundborne vibration from “rapid transit/light rail” is barely perceptible at a distance of 50 feet
(74 VdB) (FTA 2018). While each building has different characteristics for structure-borne vibration,
in general, the heavier the building, the lower the levels of vibration. Additionally, community
(human) response to vibration correlates with the frequency of events, and more-frequent low-
vibration events may evoke the same response as fewer high-vibration events.

9.7.7 Stationary Noise
Stationary sources of noise occur from all types of land uses. Residential uses generate noise from
landscaping, maintenance activities, and air conditioning systems. Commercial uses generate
noise from heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) systems; loading docks; and other
sources. Industrial uses generate noise from HVAC systems, loading docks, and outdoor
machinery. Noise generated by residential or commercial uses is generally short and intermittent.
Industrial uses generate noise on a more continual basis. Stadiums, arenas, outdoor dining and
gathering areas, gas stations, car washes, fire stations, drive-throughs, swimming pool pumps,
school playgrounds, athletic and music events, and public parks are other common stationary
noise sources.

Exterior of SoFi Stadium

Stadium/Arena Noise

Large events, including sports and special events, occur throughout the City and can also generate
high noise levels at their source. The Forum, SoFi Stadium, YouTube Theatre, and Intuit Dome, as
well as their associated outdoor areas, accommodate events that generate elevated noise levels.
Event activity noise includes pedestrian, crowd, and amplified noise; stationary mechanical
equipment; outdoor activities with amplified sound and crowd noise; loading area activity; parking
lot/structure activity (vehicle engines and accelerating, doors slamming, car alarms, and people
talking); media truck/broadcast access activity (truck movements/idling and loading/unloading of

Public Facility Noise

Outdoor activities that occur on school campuses and in parks throughout the city generate
noticeable levels of noise. Noise generated on both the weekdays (from physical education classes
and sports programs) and weekends (from use of the fields and stadiums) can elevate community
noise levels somewhat during the timeframe of each particular usage.

Construction Noise

Construction activity also contributes to the noise environment; however, such activities are
typically temporary, occurring in any one location and only for a relatively limited period of time.
Larger or multiphase construction projects, however, may contribute to the noise environment of
a particular location for a more extended period of time. Public infrastructure that requires open-
ended maintenance may also result in ongoing noise impacts, though usually not at a constant
location. For example, different sections of road may be repaved at different times, meaning that
noise impacts from associated construction activities would, at any given time, only occur along
and near the section of roadway undergoing such maintenance.

9.8 Findings
9.8.1 Public Comments
This section summarizes initial public feedback on environmental topics gathered from the
engagement activities described in Chapter 1. The comments provide insight into community
perceptions of what is missing, what needs improvement, and what is currently working well in
Inglewood, guiding future planning considerations.

In the environment and health category, seven comments raised concerns about noise from
outdoor events and aircraft; four mentioned a lack of green spaces and vegetation (including
trees); four focused on the desire for clean energy solutions like solar power; and one comment
highlighted air quality concerns. These issues were identified as needing improvement, with two
additional comments emphasizing the lack of green spaces in the city.

Regarding future visions for Inglewood, four comments proposed increased vegetation and
landscaping, three supported greater clean energy usage, one mentioned better air quality, one
suggested a more efficient water runoff and rainwater capture system, and one called for
improved noise conditions.

In terms of what works well today, four comments highlighted existing green spaces, with two
specifically mentioning Inglewood Park Cemetery as a valuable green space. One comment
praised the current air quality, and two indicated that noise pollution in Inglewood is better than
in neighboring cities.
